title: Is the Achology Knowledge Hub available for free to read?
content:
So is the Knowledge Hub genuinely free, or is there a catch? It is free. The Achology Knowledge Hub is open to anyone: its articles, quotes and book notes are public pages, with no membership, no account and no payment required. The downloadable workbooks are free too, given in exchange for an email address rather than a fee.

What you can read without paying

The Hub gathers five kinds of content in one place: articles, book notes, quotes, workbooks and author biographies, organised into seven categories and cross-linked by tag, so you can browse by the subject you are interested in, the problem you are facing, or the approach you want to learn. All of it is readable in full. Nothing is trimmed to a preview and nothing sits behind a sign-up wall.

What Achology does charge for

What is paid for is the courses, the school bundles, and community membership. The line between them is not arbitrary. A library can give you understanding, and the Hub is built to do that properly. What it cannot give you is practice with a real person and honest feedback on how it went, and that is what the courses and the community exist for.

So if a piece of writing in the Hub leads you toward a course on the same subject, that is an invitation rather than a wall. You are free to keep reading and never buy anything.

Why it is free at all

Open access is not a marketing decision made recently. It follows from one of Achology's ten value commitments, which is to ensure equitable and affordable access to training in applied psychology. The same commitment is why there is a free membership tier with real access rather than a trial, and why members offer complimentary coaching to people outside the community.

Seen together, those three things are the same idea in three forms: a library anyone can read, a membership anyone can join without paying, and coaching offered to people who are not members at all.

How it differs from these help pages

The Hub is for learning; the help section you are reading now answers support and pre-purchase questions. The two are kept apart deliberately, because somebody exploring a topic and somebody resolving a billing problem want very different things from a page. The Hub also has its own search, which covers its categories rather than these articles.

If you are weighing up whether to go further than reading, membership first or a course first is the practical next question, and what Achology actually is gives the wider picture.

title: What exactly is the Achology Knowledge Hub?
content:
So what is the Knowledge Hub, and how does it differ from these help pages? The Achology Knowledge Hub is Achology's free library of applied psychology learning content, and it lives at /learn/. It gathers several kinds of writing in one place, organised so you can find your way around by subject rather than needing to know exactly what you are looking for.

What it holds

  • Articles: applied psychology explained and put to work on real situations.
  • Book notes: what a significant book argues, and what is usable from it.
  • Quotes: single ideas with the thinking behind them set out.
  • Workbooks: downloadable exercises to work through rather than read.
  • Author biographies: who the thinkers behind the ideas actually were, with everything drawn from their work gathered on one page.

Every piece sits in one of seven categories, which are Psychology, Helping People, Mental Wellness, Motivation, Personal Growth, Wisdom for Life and General Interest, and everything is cross-linked by tag as well, so you can follow the outcome you want, the problem you are facing or the approach you want to learn across categories. The Hub has its own search, covering its own content.

How it differs from the help section

The Hub is for learning. The help section you are reading now answers support and pre-purchase questions, from what things cost to how to reach support.

The two are kept apart deliberately, because somebody exploring a subject and somebody resolving a billing problem want completely different things from a page. Mixing them would make both worse: the learning content would be interrupted by administration, and the answers would be buried in essays.

What the writing in it is like

The Hub is where Achology's teaching philosophy is most visible, because nothing there is gated or assessed. It takes the same positions the courses take: principles rather than technique lists, humanistic and evidence-informed models rather than a single school, and a deliberate avoidance of diagnostic labelling.

That is also what makes it a fair way to judge Achology. Anyone weighing it against a large course marketplace can read a great deal of the actual thinking first, at no cost, and decide whether it holds up.

Why a free library exists at all

The Hub is entirely free to read, with no account required, and that follows from one of Achology's ten value commitments: equitable and affordable access to training in applied psychology.

The same commitment is why there is a free membership tier with real access rather than a trial, and why members offer complimentary coaching to people outside the community. A library anyone can read is that belief in its plainest form.

Where the Hub stops, and what comes after it

Reading builds understanding, and the Hub is built to do that properly. What no library can give you is practice with a real person and honest feedback on how it went.

That is what the courses and community membership are for, and it is the line between what is free and what is paid. If a piece of writing in the Hub leads you toward a course on the same subject, that is an invitation rather than a wall, and membership first or a course first is the practical next question.

title: What are the major milestones in Achology's history?
content:
So how did Achology get from one course to where it is now? Achology's story begins in 2012, when Kain Ramsay published what is described as the world's first video-based psychology course. The learning platform itself was founded in 2014, and the original company, the Academy of Modern Applied Psychology, was founded in 2017.

From there it grew into a global applied-psychology platform with more than 670,000 students in its database today. The milestones below are less a list of dates than a single, consistent direction: from one course, toward a global, accredited, community-based way of learning.

The milestones along the way

  • 2012: the world's first video-based psychology course is published, the foundation of what became Achology.
  • 2014: the Achology learning platform is founded, with 12 courses.
  • 2015: the curriculum expands to 17 interlinked courses.
  • 2016: live online skill and competency development workshops begin, the first sign of the community model to come.
  • 2017: a landmark year, reaching 100,000 students, with a bespoke platform build begun and the exclusive Skilled Helper course launched with Prof. Gerard Egan.
  • 2019: the Diploma Course in Modern Applied Psychology (DiMAP), the flagship course, launches.
  • 2020: the shift to online learning accelerates worldwide, and the platform meets the demand at scale.
  • 2021: the community learning system is upgraded and gains continuing professional development (CPD) accreditation, with 350,000 total enrolled students.
  • 2022: half a million students reached worldwide, with the curriculum grown to 25 courses.
  • 2023: the version 2 community portal launches with the current 28-course curriculum.
  • 2024: the Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP) is founded by Master Achologists, to raise integrity standards in the field.
  • 2025: a full migration to Circle gives Achology its permanent online home.
  • 2025 to 2026: an Eldership team is established and free learning is opened to the public, with 670,000+ students in the database.

How to read the dates

It is worth separating two threads that often get muddled. The brand's public story begins in 2012 with that first course, while the founding of the original company was 2017. An older claim that Achology was founded in 2015 is simply incorrect, and Achology would rather say so than let it stand.

What actually runs through the whole timeline is one consistent move: from selling single courses, toward accreditation, community, and now free public learning through the Knowledge Hub. The fullest picture of where that arrived is in What is Achology?

title: What are the registered company details of Achology?
content:
So what are the registered details, if you need them for an invoice or a formal request? Achology trades through two companies registered in Scotland: Achology Transactions Ltd, Scottish company number SC697126, and the Academy of Modern Applied Psychology Ltd, Scottish company number SC612822. Achology is the trading name both operate under.

The registered details in full

  • Achology Transactions Ltd (ATL): Scottish company number SC697126.
  • The Academy of Modern Applied Psychology Ltd (AMAP): Scottish company number SC612822.
  • Registered office for both companies: Clyde Offices, 2nd Floor, 48 West George Street, Glasgow, Scotland, G2 1BP.

Which of the two applies to you

It depends on what you bought and when. Courses and bundles, and community subscriptions taken from 1 June 2023 onward, are with Achology Transactions Ltd. Community subscriptions bought before that date are with the Academy of Modern Applied Psychology Ltd.

Nothing about your rights changes between the two. The refund policy, the law that governs the terms and your rights as a customer apply the same way whichever company holds your contract.

When you would actually need these

Most people never do. They matter when something needs to be formal rather than conversational: putting a purchase through an employer's expenses or training budget, raising an invoice, making a records or data request, or writing to Achology about a contractual matter. In each of those cases the registered name, company number and registered office are what the other side is asking for.

Why any of this is published at all

A registered company number is checkable by anyone, at source, in the Companies House register, without asking Achology for anything. That is the point of publishing it. It sits alongside registration on the UK Register of Learning Providers and independent verification of every professional development claim as the three things about Achology that can be confirmed without taking anyone's word for it.

For an organisation teaching applied psychology, where a reader is being asked to judge whether training is real and substantial, being verifiable from the outside matters more than any claim made on a page. What Achology actually is sets out the wider picture, and how the trust and legal policies fit together covers how the documents relate.

title: With which Achology company am I formally contracting?
content:
So who are you actually entering a contract with when you buy? It depends on what you bought and when. Courses and course bundles, and community subscriptions taken on or after 1 June 2023, are with Achology Transactions Ltd. Community subscriptions bought before 1 June 2023 are with the Academy of Modern Applied Psychology Ltd. Achology is the trading name both companies operate under.

The simple version

  • Courses and course bundles: Achology Transactions Ltd (ATL).
  • Community subscriptions from 1 June 2023 onward: Achology Transactions Ltd.
  • Community subscriptions bought before 1 June 2023: the Academy of Modern Applied Psychology Ltd (AMAP).

Why there are two companies at all

The split is a matter of history rather than anything to read into. The Academy of Modern Applied Psychology was the original company, founded in 2017, and it still holds the community subscriptions taken out under it. Achology Transactions Ltd was established later to handle course sales and, from June 2023, new community subscriptions. Both are registered in Scotland and share one registered office in Glasgow. Achology's history sets out how the organisation grew into that shape.

What it changes for you, which is very little

This is the part worth being plain about, because two company names on a receipt can look like something to worry about. Nothing about what you are entitled to changes between them.

The 14-day money-back guarantee on courses applies the same way, refunds are requested through the same process, the same law governs the terms, and your rights as a customer are identical. Your access, your courses and your progress record are unaffected.

When the answer actually matters

It matters when a document has to name the right legal entity: an invoice for an employer or a training budget, a formal records or data request, or correspondence about a contract. In those cases you need the registered name and company number, and the registered company details lists both companies, their Scottish company numbers and the shared registered office.

If the question behind your question is really about a purchase you are reconsidering, the refund policy is the more useful page, and how the trust and legal policies work together shows how the documents fit around each other.

title: What does the Coaching HOT Seat entail?
content:
So what actually happens in a Coaching HOT Seat, and what is it like to sit in one? The Coaching HOT Seat is one of the six Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS) types, and it is a live coaching demonstration. One member takes the seat with a real challenge or goal, up to three Achologists coach them in turn, and the rest of the group observes.

What actually happens in it

The person in the seat brings something genuine they are working through, not a tidy example invented for practice. The coaching then happens in real time, in front of everyone.

That is what makes it valuable and slightly daunting in equal measure. For the observers, watching skilled coaching up close, and seeing how a good coach handles a real person, is one of the fastest ways to improve their own practice.

Up to three Achologists coach in turn, so you also see different styles brought to the same problem, and how each reads the person in front of them slightly differently.

What it is like to sit in the seat

Taking the seat yourself is the part members are often nervous about and glad they did. You bring a real issue and receive focused coaching from several practitioners, with the group's attention on the work rather than on you.

Most people find it far more supportive than exposing, and leave with something they can actually use.

How credit works

The roles earn different credit. The coaches earn a Peer-Peer Applied Learning Session (PALS) credit for coaching, the person in the seat earns a PALS received, and the observers earn a VALTS credit for attending.

Why members rate it

Coaching in public asks a different quality of performance than a private session: you cannot hide a hesitation, and you see how others handle the same moment. That is why the HOT Seat is one of the alternative PALS formats required at the senior levels, and why many members point to it as where their coaching genuinely sharpened. Once qualified, you can host your own, and it counts among the events that earn accreditation credit.

title: What is the process for submitting a CPD claim after participating?
content:
So what do you do after the session to make sure it counts? You submit a claim through the member self-report form. You are also invited to record a short takeaway from the session while still on the group call. The Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP) then reviews the claim and records the credit against your account.

The steps, in order

  • Attend or host the event.
  • Record your short takeaway while still on the call, if the host invites one.
  • Submit the claim through the member self-report form, naming the event and the role you took.
  • Wait for verification. The credit appears on your record once it is confirmed, not before.

The role matters, because it decides which credit you receive: attending earns one kind, delivering or hosting another, and how the credit splits by role sets out the difference.

Why the credit is not instant

Hosts will not tell you a credit has been recorded, because at that moment it has not been. Verification is a separate step, done by somebody other than you, and it takes as long as it takes.

That delay is the process working rather than the system running slowly. No self-reported activity enters the official record until an independent body has checked it, and a record that updated the instant a member claimed something would be a record nobody had checked. What makes an Achology standing worth anything to an employer or a client is precisely that they do not have to take your word for it.

The habit that prevents trouble

Submit as you go. Unsubmitted work is invisible to the system no matter how much of it you have done, and the most common disappointment on the pathway is a member who has genuinely done the activity, whose own checklist looks healthy, and whose level does not arrive because the claims were never made.

Treat the checklist as your plan and the verified record as your score. Doing the activity is most of the effort; claiming it is what turns effort into progress.

Where the verified credit lives

Confirmed credit is added to your official record in the Achology Member Data Centre, which tracks activity across every member level. That record is what you draw on when you need to evidence your progression to somebody outside Achology, and it is what stands behind a certificate of achievement as distinct from a certificate of completion.

title: What steps should I follow to organise my own Achology event?
content:
So how do you go about hosting an event of your own? Once you reach Achologist level and complete the host training for Virtual Achologist Led Training Sessions (VALTS), formally the Group Facilitation and VALTS Host Training, you can host five credit-earning event types with no further approval: the Skill Development Workshop, the Principle-Based Reflective Discussion, the Case Study-Based Discussion Group, the Coaching HOT Seat, and the Live Coaching Practice, Observation and Feedback session.

Hosting an Achologist-Led Tutorial requires Achologist Adept, and a few events are hosted only by the Eldership team.

The six steps to publish one

Every event uses a locked template, so each one reads consistently regardless of who is hosting. The only part you write yourself is a short Theme of This Specific Event paragraph naming what your session covers.

1. Open the Host a Live Event space on Circle and find your event in the Event Descriptions Library.

2. Copy the full template.

3. Start a direct message to a member of the Eldership team.

4. Paste the template into the message.

5. Write your Theme of This Specific Event paragraph at the top.

6. Send it. The Eldership member approves it, publishes it, and adds the event image.

That is genuinely the whole process. The template exists so that hosting your first event is a matter of describing your theme rather than designing a session from nothing.

Hosting community events

The community events, the ones carrying no credit, sit in a second tier reached by informal invitation from the Eldership team rather than application. Readiness is recognised through sustained participation in the facilitation mentorship group and the host training. Once invited, you publish them the same way.

Remember that hosting earns you a Peer-Peer Applied Learning Session (PALS) credit, and that you still submit the claim afterwards like any other activity. Whether members can host their own workshops is covered separately for anyone still deciding.

title: Which Achology events qualify for accreditation credit?
content:
So which events count toward your progression, and which are simply worth attending? Nine of Achology's 22 event types earn accreditation credit. They are the events governed by the Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP), the independent body that verifies members' professional development. The other 13, the general community events and mentorship groups, carry no credit in any role.

The six that earn a session credit

  • Skill Development Workshop
  • Principle-Based Reflective Discussion
  • Case Study-Based Discussion Group
  • The Coaching HOT Seat
  • Achologist-Led Tutorial
  • Live Coaching Practice, Observation and Feedback Session

Attending one earns a Virtual Achologist Led Training Session (VALTS) credit. Hosting or taking a coaching role earns a Peer-Peer Applied Learning Session (PALS) credit instead, because that is delivery rather than attendance.

The three that count differently

  • The Code of Ethics Training and the Code of Character and Conduct Training earn no session credit. Attending keeps your two compliance strands current, which is required for progression at all.
  • The Group Facilitation and VALTS Host Training is the gateway event: completing it qualifies you to host, and so to start earning credit for delivery.

What the other 13 are for

It would be a mistake to read the split as valuable against not valuable. The community events and mentorship groups carry no credit because they are not assessed activities, not because they matter less. They are where members find people working on the same things, and the mentorship groups in particular are where readiness to host is usually recognised.

What the distinction is actually for is honesty about the record. A credit says an independent body confirmed you did something specific, in a specific role. Attending a discussion because you enjoyed it is real, and it is not the same claim.

How to plan around it

Knowing the nine matters when you are working toward a level with a fixed requirement, since each level asks for a certain number of sessions across a certain spread of types. A year spent entirely in community events would leave your record where it started.

If you are unsure what suits where you are now, choosing the right event for your level is the practical guide, the full list of live events covers all 22, and every credit is claimed and verified afterwards rather than awarded automatically.

title: What does the DiMAP course upgrade include?
content:
So what does the upgrade give you that the diploma on its own does not? The Diploma Course in Modern Applied Psychology (DiMAP) has an upgrade bundle of its own. The DiMAP Course Upgrade pairs the diploma with twelve months of Achology Membership, for $399. It is an upgrade on buying the diploma by itself, which is $299 and comes with three months of complimentary membership. So the real question the upgrade answers is not "which course" but "how long do I want to be part of the community while I study it".

What DiMAP itself is

DiMAP is Achology's flagship course and the foundation the rest of the catalogue builds on: it appears in all seven schools and runs to more than fifty hours of material. It is also the course the continuing professional development (CPD) pathway requires by Senior Achologist I, so for anyone heading toward accreditation, it is not optional. That is why it is the course most often bought first, and the one the upgrade is built around.

What you get for the difference

For $100 more than the course alone, the upgrade extends your community membership from three months to a full twelve. That is the whole of the difference, and it is worth seeing plainly: membership on its own is $34.50 a month, so nine extra months bought this way is straightforward value if you are going to use them.

Membership is where the practising side of the pathway happens, the live events, the coaching board, the mentorship groups, and the community the CPD pathway runs through.

Who it suits, and who it does not

The upgrade suits someone who already knows they want to stay engaged with the community for the year and work toward accreditation: for them, the twelve included months are better value than paying month to month once the complimentary period ends.

It suits you less well if you mainly want the diploma itself and are not yet sure about the community. In that case the standard course, with its three complimentary months, lets you try the community before committing to a year, and you keep lifetime access to the course either way.

title: What are the three learning paths offered by Achology?
content:
So where do you start if you do not yet know which course you want? Achology groups its courses into three high-level learning paths, a simpler way to find your direction than working through all 28 courses one by one. They are Mental Health and Wellbeing, Personal Growth and Development, and Applied Psychology Certification. Some courses sit in more than one path, because the same learning can serve more than one goal.

What each path is for

  • Mental Health and Wellbeing: courses focused on understanding and supporting mental health, resilience, and emotional wellbeing, both for yourself and for the people you help.
  • Personal Growth and Development: courses focused on confidence, communication, clarity, productivity, and personal effectiveness, for people who want to grow in their own lives and work.
  • Applied Psychology Certification: the Practitioner Certification courses that are required for continuing professional development (CPD) progression toward Achologist status and beyond.

How to choose between them

The honest way to use the paths is to start from why you are here, not from the course list. If your aim is professional practice and accreditation, the Applied Psychology Certification path holds the courses the pathway actually counts, so that is where to look first.

If you want to support your own or others' mental health, the Mental Health and Wellbeing path points you at the courses built for that. If your aim is personal growth in your work and relationships, the Personal Growth path is the one.

Someone training to coach professionally and someone wanting to steady their own life will pick different starting points, and the paths exist to make that first choice obvious.

How paths relate to schools

The paths and the seven schools are two views of the same catalogue. A path groups courses by the goal you are pursuing; a school groups them by subject.

They are a way of choosing where to start, not fixed tracks you are locked into, and you are free to take courses from more than one path. If you would rather not choose at all, the school bundles and the Access All Areas option give you whole groups at once.

title: Are there Achology courses that are included in multiple bundles?
content:
So can the same course turn up in more than one bundle you buy? Yes. Several courses are shared across more than one school bundle, because some subjects genuinely belong to more than one field, Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP) and Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) among them. The clearest example is the Diploma Course in Modern Applied Psychology (DiMAP), which appears in all seven schools as the foundational course the rest build on.

The shared courses

  • Diploma Course in Modern Applied Psychology (DiMAP): in all seven schools.
  • Mindset Mastery: The Ultimate NLP-Based Guide to Self-Discovery: in the NLP school and the Mental Health school.
  • Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Mental Health and Wellness: in the Cognitive Behavioural Psychology (CBP) school and the Mental Health school.
  • The Skilled Helper Training Course (with Prof. Gerard Egan): in the Life Coaching school and the Person-Centred school.
  • Mindfulness for Mental Health, Personal Growth and Inner Peace: in the Mindfulness school and the Mental Health school.
  • Mindfulness for Highly Efficient Management and Leadership: in the Mindfulness school and the Personal Growth school.
  • The Clarity, Purpose and Personal Effectiveness Masterclass: in the Life Coaching, Mindfulness and Personal Growth schools.
  • The Strategic Goal Setting and Action Planning Masterclass: in the CBP school and the Personal Growth school.
  • The Communication Skills and Social Intelligence Masterclass: in the Person-Centred school and the Personal Growth school.

Why the overlap exists

It would be tidier to file every course under exactly one heading, and it would also be false. Cognitive behavioural work genuinely belongs both to its own tradition and to mental health practice. Mindfulness belongs both to contemplative practice and to leadership. Forcing a single home on each course would make the catalogue look neater and describe the subject less accurately.

DiMAP sits in all seven for a stronger reason still: it is the foundation the rest assume. That is also why the pathway requires it by Senior Achologist I, whichever field you are heading into.

What this means when you buy

If you buy more than one school, a shared course may appear in both, and you lose nothing by it: you keep lifetime access to the course either way, and you are not charged twice for the same material within a bundle's price.

What it does mean is that two bundles are not always twice the content. If you are choosing between school bundles, it is worth looking at the overlap before assuming the second one doubles what you have.

If you would rather not track any of this

The Access All Areas Pass includes all 28 courses once, with no overlaps to work out, and twelve months of membership. How the school bundles work covers buying by field instead, and the three learning paths are the simpler way in if you are still deciding on a direction rather than a subject.

title: What courses are part of each Achology school bundle?
content:
So what do you actually get in each school bundle? Each of Achology's seven schools is a bundle of courses in one field. Six of the schools hold five or six courses; the School of Personal Growth and Development holds twelve. The Diploma Course in Modern Applied Psychology (DiMAP) is shared across all seven, because it is the foundational course the whole catalogue builds on.

A note on the figures below: because some courses appear in more than one school, the student totals count those shared courses under each school, so they overlap rather than sum.

The seven schools and their courses

  • School of Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP), 5 courses, 162+ hours: DiMAP, A Beginner's Guide to Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP), Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP) Practitioner Training, Neuro-Linguistic Programming Master Practitioner Course, and Mindset Mastery.
  • School of Cognitive Behavioural Psychology (CBP), 5 courses, 121+ hours: DiMAP, Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) Practitioner Course, The CBT Toolkit, Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Mental Health and Wellness, and The Strategic Goal Setting and Action Planning Masterclass.
  • School of Life Coaching and Professional Helping, 6 courses, 150+ hours: DiMAP, Life Coaching Certificate Course (Beginner to Advanced), Life Coaching Blueprint, The Skilled Helper Training Course (with Prof. Gerard Egan), Skilled Helper Practitioner Course (Advanced to Expert), and The Clarity, Purpose and Personal Effectiveness Masterclass.
  • School of Person-Centred Counselling and Psychology, 5 courses, 145+ hours: DiMAP, Hypnotherapy Practitioner Course, Counselling Skills Practitioner Course, The Skilled Helper Training Course (with Prof. Gerard Egan), and The Communication Skills and Social Intelligence Masterclass.
  • School of Mindfulness, Applied Insight and Wisdom (MIW), 5 courses, 121+ hours: DiMAP, Mindfulness Practitioner Diploma Course, Mindfulness for Mental Health, Personal Growth and Inner Peace, Mindfulness for Highly Efficient Management and Leadership, and The Clarity, Purpose and Personal Effectiveness Masterclass.
  • School of Mental Health, Wellness and Emotional Resilience, 5 courses, 131+ hours: DiMAP, Mental Health and Wellbeing Practitioner Diploma Course, Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Mental Health and Wellness, Mindfulness for Mental Health, Personal Growth and Inner Peace, and Mindset Mastery.
  • School of Personal Growth and Development (PGD), 12 courses, 183+ hours: DiMAP plus eleven personal-development courses spanning self-belief, confidence, emotional intelligence, clarity and purpose, goal setting, communication, productivity, mental toughness, relationships, leadership-focused mindfulness, and entrepreneurship.

Buying a school

Each school bundle includes its courses plus twelve months of Achology Membership, and works out cheaper than buying the same courses separately.

If you want everything, the Access All Areas Pass includes all 28 courses across all seven schools.

title: What is the total number of courses offered by Achology?
content:
So how many courses are there, and how are they organised? Achology offers 28 individual courses in total, grouped into seven schools of applied psychology, each school gathering the courses that belong to one field. They range from short, focused masterclasses of ten to sixteen hours up to full practitioner diploma courses, so the catalogue holds both a first taste of a subject and a complete professional training in it.

How the 28 are organised

The seven schools are the School of Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP), the School of Cognitive Behavioural Psychology (CBP), the School of Life Coaching and Professional Helping, the School of Person-Centred Counselling and Psychology, the School of Mindfulness, Applied Insight and Wisdom (MIW), the School of Mental Health, Wellness and Emotional Resilience, and the School of Personal Growth and Development (PGD). Because some subjects genuinely belong to more than one field, a single course can sit in more than one school, so the schools' totals add up to more than 28.

The clearest example is the Diploma Course in Modern Applied Psychology (DiMAP), the foundational course that appears in all seven.

Where to start among 28

Twenty-eight is a lot to face at once, so most people do not choose a course so much as choose a direction. If you are new, the three learning paths are the simplest way in, grouping the catalogue by goal rather than by subject.

If you already know the field you want, each school bundle collects its courses in one place. And the foundational diploma, DiMAP, is where a great many members begin, because it underpins the rest.

Ways to buy them

You can take a course on its own, buy a whole school as a bundle, or take the Access All Areas Pass, which includes all 28 courses. Whichever route you choose, the courses themselves are identical; the difference is only how many you gain access to at once, and the fuller cost picture sets out what each option costs.

title: If I request a refund on a course, will I lose my free membership?
content:
So if you refund a course, does the membership that came with it disappear too? No. Refunding a course does not, by itself, cancel the complimentary Achology Membership that came with it. The two are handled separately, so if you refund a course within the 14-day money-back guarantee and you do not want the membership to continue either, you need to cancel the membership yourself.

What to do, in order

  • Request the course refund through the usual refund process, within 14 days of purchase.
  • Cancel the membership inside the community platform, Circle, which stops all future payments.
  • Do both at the same time, so nothing is left running quietly in the background.

Why this catches people out

A course bought from Achology comes with three months of complimentary membership. Cancel nothing and, when those three months end, the membership continues automatically at $34.50 a month.

So somebody who refunds a course, assumes everything attached to it has gone, and hears nothing for three months can be surprised by a charge they were not expecting. Cancelling at the same time as the refund removes that entirely.

Why the two are separate in the first place

They are separate because they are different kinds of thing. A course is a one-off purchase of material you keep, which is why it carries a 14-day guarantee: you can look at it, decide it is not for you, and hand it back.

Membership is not a thing you own but access you are using from the moment it starts, to live events, the coaching board and the community. That is why membership is non-refundable once access has begun while remaining cancellable at any time. You are not tied in; you simply are not refunded for access you have already had.

If you are stepping away entirely

Request the course refund and cancel the membership, and nothing further will be charged. Anything you have already earned toward a member level is unaffected by either action, and what happens to your progress if you leave covers where that record stands.

If the reason for the refund is something that might be fixable, a technical problem and disagreeing with course content are each treated on their own terms, and the refund policy sets out the whole position.

title: My course included free membership. What happens when it ends?
content:
So what happens when the free membership that came with your course runs out? It does not simply stop. A course purchase comes with three months of complimentary Achology Membership, and when those three months end the membership continues automatically at the standard rate of $34.50 a month until you cancel it. You can cancel at any time inside the community platform, Circle, which stops all future payments.

What you need to do, either way

  • To keep your community access: nothing. It carries on and you are billed monthly once the complimentary period ends.
  • To stop it: cancel before the three months are up, and no payment is taken.
  • Either way, the course you bought is unaffected. Cancelling stops future payments; it does not remove the lifetime access to the course itself.

Why the membership continues rather than lapsing

This is the part worth understanding rather than being caught by. The three months are not a trial of a product you might later buy. They are the community half of what you already bought, and it runs on from the first day.

Course study and community membership are two different things. The course gives you the material. The community is where the practice happens: the live events, the coaching board, the peer sessions and the mentorship that membership includes. Including three months with every course is how Achology puts the two together rather than selling study on its own, since study without practice does not produce a practitioner.

Whether that continues is genuinely your call, and it is a single click either way.

Two things that catch people out

The complimentary period is longer with some purchases. The Access All Areas Pass includes twelve months rather than three, as do the school bundles, so the date you are watching for is not always three months out.

And membership is non-refundable once access has started, because that access begins immediately. If you decide it is not for you, cancelling to stop future payments is the route, rather than asking for a month already under way to be returned. If you are refunding the course as well, the two are handled separately and both need doing.

If you are deciding whether to keep it

Monthly against annual sets out the cost either way, and the mentoring that comes with membership is the part course buyers most often underestimate.

title: How do monthly and annual Achology memberships differ?
content:
So should you pay monthly or annually, and what is the real difference? The difference between monthly and annual Achology Membership is how you pay and how much you save. Monthly is $7 for your first 30 days, then $34.50 a month, billed each month until you cancel. Annual is $345 for a full year, paid once. Both give you exactly the same access to the community; the only thing that changes is the commitment and the cost.

What each one costs

  • Monthly: $7 for the first 30 days, then $34.50 per month, cancellable at any time to stop future payments.
  • Annual: $345 per year, which works out at roughly two months free compared with paying monthly for a year, and renews annually unless you cancel before the renewal date.

What that access actually contains

Whichever plan you choose, membership is where the practising side of Achology happens: access to courses, unlimited live sessions, structured mentorship, the coaching board, daily discussion groups, and the networking that runs through it all. It is the difference between owning a course and taking part in a community, which is worth being clear about before you choose a plan: membership and courses are not the same purchase.

Which one to choose

The monthly plan, with its $7 first month, is the low-commitment way in: sensible if you want to try the community or are not yet sure how long you will stay. The annual plan is the better value if you already know you want to be part of Achology for the year, since it saves you about two months' worth of payments. One honest point either way: membership is non-refundable once your access starts, because that access begins immediately, though you can cancel at any time to stop future payments. So if you are unsure, the monthly trial is the gentler place to begin, and the free tier is gentler still.

title: Is there a free Achology membership tier, and what does it include?
content:
So can you join Achology without paying anything, and what do you actually get? Yes. There is a free membership tier and it needs no payment to join. It is a real membership with genuine access rather than a preview screen: free events through the week, the coaching board, the discussion forum, and the quarterly live Code of Ethics training.

What the free membership includes

  • The events calendar, with free events running Monday to Friday, excluding holidays.
  • The coaching board, where you can apply for one-to-one coaching sessions offered by subscribing members.
  • The discussion forum, where you can ask questions of Society of Modern Applied Psychology (SoMAP) members and the Achology Eldership.
  • The quarterly live Code of Ethics training.

What your first week can look like

Join a free event, post to the coaching board and apply for a session, then start reading and asking in the forum. None of that costs anything.

It is also enough to answer the question most people actually have at this stage, which is not what the features are but whether these are their kind of people and whether it is worth their time. The free tier exists so you can find that out honestly rather than from a sales page.

What it does not include, and why

The free tier does not include the courses, the unlimited live sessions, or the structured mentorship. Those sit with paid Achology Membership, at $7 for the first 30 days and then $34.50 a month.

The line is not drawn where you might expect. What is given away is the community, and what is charged for is the structured training inside it. That is the opposite of the usual arrangement, where free access means a locked room with a window in it.

Why it exists at all

Two reasons, and the second is the one worth knowing.

The first is the commitment to equitable and affordable access, the same one behind the free Knowledge Hub and complimentary coaching for people outside the community.

The second is that the free tier is load-bearing for the pathway itself. Subscribing members working toward a level need people to coach and to teach, and free members are part of who they practise with. So the arrangement is not charity in one direction: a free member receives real coaching, and a paying member receives the practice that their progression depends on.

If you are weighing up going further, membership first or a course first is the practical next question and the fuller cost picture sets out every option.

title: Which professional standards apply to a trainee Achologist?
content:
So what is expected of you while you are still training? Trainee Achologists, meaning members still working through a practitioner qualification course, hold to the same ethical framework as qualified members, with a few added responsibilities that reflect where they are. The central one is honesty about status: a trainee tells clients, or makes sure they know, that they are training.

What trainees commit to

  • Tell clients you are a trainee. After qualifying, whether to disclose past trainee status becomes a matter of professional judgement.
  • Get permission before using any client work for educational purposes, with identities thoroughly anonymised, and treat consent as mandatory wherever anonymity cannot be guaranteed.
  • Provide services that meet the framework's professional, moral and ethical standards.
  • Work with reasonable care and skill, collaborating with senior practitioners and professional advisors.
  • Stay mindful of any conflict between obligations, such as to other clients or to a training provider, and seek guidance.
  • Talk honestly with trusted members of the community about your training, your client work and your ethical practice.

Why disclosure comes first

Of the six, telling clients you are training is the one everything else rests on, and it is the one trainees find hardest. Saying it out loud can feel like an admission of not being good enough yet.

It is the opposite. A person deciding whether to work with you is entitled to know what they are agreeing to, and a trainee who says so is demonstrating exactly the honesty the framework asks for. Most people, told plainly, are entirely willing. What they object to is finding out later.

How the pathway protects the people you practise on

The standards are not the only safeguard, which is worth knowing if practising while still learning sounds uncomfortable. The structure itself is built so that you practise on the people best able to absorb it first.

You receive coaching as a client before delivering any. Peer coaching comes next, with fellow members who understand the learning context. Only at Senior Achologist I does coaching people outside the community begin, by which point you have completed courses, been coached repeatedly and received structured feedback on your own practice.

Where these standards sit

They are additions to, not replacements for, the commitments every practising Achologist makes to clients, and they assume the character traits the community expects throughout.

Two of the six, seeking guidance and talking honestly with other members, are not restrictions at all. They describe the ordinary use of a learning community, and the mentoring available with membership is where most trainees find them.

title: What are my commitments as a practising Achologist?
content:
So what exactly are you committing to when you start working with clients? As a practising Achologist serving the public you commit to five ethical standards, which come from the Achology Code of Ethics. Meeting them is a condition of standing as a member.

The five commitments

  • Always put the client's needs first, ahead of your own interests.
  • Work to a high standard, keeping your professional development current so your practice stays sharp.
  • Work within your competencies, and be honest about them in relation to a client's situation.
  • Maintain healthy, honouring relationships, held with unconditional positive regard, authenticity and empathy.
  • Maintain confidentiality, privacy and trust, never disclosing a client's information without consent or genuine necessity.

The third one is the difficult one

Four of the five read as things any decent practitioner would agree to without argument. Working within your competencies is the one that costs something, because it means saying no.

Somebody arrives with a difficulty that is outside what you are trained for, or beyond what coaching can reach. They are in front of you, they want help, and you could try. The commitment says be honest about your competence in relation to their situation, which in practice means telling them this is not the right place and, where you can, saying where might be.

That is also why the second commitment exists alongside it. Keeping your development current is what widens the range of situations you can genuinely take on, rather than widening what you are willing to attempt.

What sits alongside the five

The code adds several practical duties. When you offer services to the public you make sure appropriate insurance is in place, and you hold the same standards whether you work online or in person. You are also expected to be accountable, meaning ready to explain how you have met your obligations if asked.

All of it exists for one purpose: protecting the client's interests and their capacity to decide for themselves. That last part matters. The commitments are not written to make you cautious. They are written so the person in front of you stays the one making decisions about their own life.

How these connect to the rest of the framework

The five commitments are the Code of Ethics in its most usable form, expressing the same values as the ten value commitments and the nine value-based principles, which are what you reach for when two obligations pull against each other.

They assume the character traits expected of an Achologist, they are kept current through annual ethics training, and they apply with added care while you are still training, which the standards for a trainee Achologist sets out.

title: What are the seven signs of maturity that Achology teaches?
content:
So what does Achology mean when it calls someone mature? The seven marks of maturity come from the Code of Ethics, in a section on the essence of maturity, and they describe a mature person as someone whose decisions are rooted in values rather than in passing emotions or opinions. They give members a picture of the character the whole framework is trying to help them grow toward.

The seven marks

  • Keeps long-term commitments, delaying gratification and honouring commitments even when they are uninspiring.
  • Is indifferent to flattery or criticism, holding a secure identity that is not shaken by external opinion.
  • Possesses a spirit of humility, honouring others and acknowledging their contributions.
  • Makes decisions based on character, acting proactively rather than looking for excuses.
  • Can prioritise self last, contributing to others' wellbeing in a balanced, discerning way.
  • Seeks wisdom before acting, keeping a teachable spirit and valuing counsel from the wise.
  • Consistently expresses gratitude.

What they are describing

Notice what is absent from that list. There is nothing about age, qualifications, confidence or success. Every one of the seven is about where a person's decisions come from when circumstances are not helping.

The second is the one members most often stop at. Indifference to flattery or criticism does not mean not caring what anyone thinks. It means holding an identity steady enough that praise does not inflate it and criticism does not collapse it, which for anyone who intends to sit with other people's difficulties is not a luxury but a working requirement.

Why maturity is written into an ethical framework at all

Because in helping work, technique is not the thing that fails first. A practitioner who needs the client's approval, who cannot delay their own gratification, or who is unteachable, will make poor decisions with perfectly good methods.

That is the reasoning behind Achology treating character as trainable rather than assumed, set out in why Achology emphasises character development, and it is why the marks are offered as a description to grow into rather than a test to pass. Nobody meets all seven consistently.

How they connect to everything else

The marks are one of four related pictures of the same person. They line up with the nine value-based principles, where Maturity in Character is itself named as one of the nine, and with the 22 character traits the Code of Ethics sets out.

Where those are aspirational, the nine virtues of the Code of Character and Conduct are the strand that is actually trained and tracked, through live sessions on a rolling requirement. Read together they say the same thing in four registers: what to aspire to, what to decide by, what to become, and what gets practised.

title: What are Achology's nine value-based principles?
content:
So what are the nine principles, and how do you use them when a decision is hard? The nine value-based principles are how Achology's Code of Ethics turns its values into something a member can actually act on. The handbook's own reasoning is that stating values as principles makes them usable at the moment a real decision has to be made.

The nine principles

  • Personal Integrity: living consistently by core principles such as honesty, fairness and decency.
  • Personal Autonomy: staying true to yourself and your own principles, free from external manipulation.
  • Unconditional Inclusion: accepting every person's full contribution, regardless of difference.
  • Altruism: serving the needs of others above personal interest, with empathy as its engine.
  • Moral Imagination: the ability to envision several options for resolving an ethical dilemma.
  • Growth Mindset: treating skills as learnable and failures as opportunities to learn.
  • Social Contribution: prioritising giving over taking within families, neighbourhoods and communities.
  • Personal Responsibility: taking ownership and acting as a role model whose influence reaches beyond you.
  • Maturity in Character: self-awareness, social awareness and the wisdom to learn from experience.

The test the handbook gives

If one or more of these principles is strongly reflected in a decision, without contradicting any other, the decision can be regarded as ethically well-founded.

That is deliberately not a rule that decides for you. It is a check that tells you whether your reasoning has anything underneath it, which is a different and more honest thing to offer a practitioner facing a situation nobody anticipated.

What it looks like in a real moment

Say a client shares something that worries you, and you find yourself wanting to intervene more firmly than they have asked you to.

Personal Integrity and Altruism both point toward acting in their interest. Unconditional Inclusion and Personal Autonomy pull the other way, reminding you they have the right to decide for themselves. Moral Imagination is the principle that stops you treating this as two options when there are usually four.

Where the principles cannot all be honoured at once, you weigh which matter most here, and you are able to say afterwards why. That weighing is the skill, and it is what the annual Code of Ethics training exists to keep sharp.

Why principles rather than rules

Rules cover situations somebody has already thought of. Helping work produces situations nobody wrote down, and a practitioner who can only follow rules is stranded the moment one appears.

This is what turns the ten value commitments from a statement of belief into a working method, and it connects directly to the seven marks of maturity, where Maturity in Character appears in both lists. The everyday form of the same values is the five community principles, and their client-facing form is the five commitments every practising Achologist makes.

title: What are the ten core value commitments of Achology?
content:
So what does Achology actually commit itself to? Ten value commitments, set out in its Code of Ethics, which bind the organisation and its members alike. They shape the goals Achology sets and the decisions it makes.

The ten commitments

  • Upholding human rights, individuality and dignity for all.
  • Actively supporting people in relieving personal suffering and distress.
  • Promoting the wellbeing, personal growth and capabilities of individuals.
  • Enhancing the quality of relationships between people, built on trust and understanding.
  • Strengthening personal resilience and effectiveness.
  • Encouraging people to embody virtuous and ethical characteristics in their interactions.
  • Maintaining the confidentiality of people's private information, prioritising their safety and wellbeing.
  • Upholding the integrity of the practitioner and client relationship in applied psychology.
  • Enhancing the usefulness of abstract psychological knowledge in practical, everyday applications.
  • Ensuring equitable and affordable access to training in applied psychology.

Where you can actually see them

A list of values is worth only as much as the things it visibly produces, so it is fair to ask where each one shows up.

The confidentiality commitment is the root of the privacy positions across the policies, and of the confidentiality standard every practising Achologist commits to with clients.

The applied-knowledge commitment, the ninth, is why the platform is built around practice rather than study alone, and why progression past the first level requires demonstrated practice rather than more completed courses.

The access commitment, the tenth, is the most visible of all. It is why the Knowledge Hub is free to read, why the free membership tier gives real access rather than a preview, and why members deliver complimentary coaching to people outside the community.

Why publish them at all

Published commitments are checkable. Anyone can read the tenth commitment and then look at what Achology charges for and what it gives away, and judge whether the two match. Values kept internal cannot be tested that way, which is most of the reason for putting them in a public document.

How they fit the wider framework

The ten commitments sit alongside the nine value-based principles, which turn these beliefs into a method for weighing a real decision, and the five community principles, which express them in daily conduct between members.

Read together they say one thing in three registers: what Achology believes, how it decides, and how members behave.

title: What is the Achology Code of Ethics (Ethical Conduct)?
content:
So what is the Code of Ethics, and what does it ask of you in practice? The Achology Code of Ethics is the framework of professional conduct that every practising Achologist works within. Its formal name is the Ethical Framework for Practitioners of Applied Psychology. It is the primary reference members use when making decisions about their own conduct, whether professional, relational, financial, or social, and adhering to it is a condition of standing as a member.

What it is grounded in

The framework is built on virtue ethics, the tradition running from Socrates and the Stoics through Aristotle, which emphasises cultivating good character over simply following rules. The handbook presents the code as an integrity health check rather than a box-ticking exercise, with the aim of helping members aspire to be better, not merely to do the right thing in the moment. Integrity is named its cornerstone virtue.

The three ways it is used

The code is not a document you read once and shelve. The handbook names three live uses for it: guiding everyday professional practice, including being open about it with a client at the outset; supporting ethical decision-making, giving you a structured way to weigh a real dilemma when two principles pull against each other; and supporting reflection, explicitly including the coaching and practice sessions on the pathway. In other words, it is meant to be used in the room, not admired on a shelf.

How it is trained and kept current

The code comes with a six-part video training course, working through moral and ethical excellence, the role of an ethically minded Achologist, the integrity health check, ongoing character development, the qualities that positively influence people, and a closing commitment to keep the practice alive. Attending the live Code of Ethics training once a year is a continuing professional development (CPD) compliance requirement from Achologist Adept onward. It is one of Achology's three conduct codes, distinct from the Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC) and the Community Code of Conduct. Its values are expressed in more usable form as the ten value commitments and the nine value-based principles.

title: What are the suggested character traits of an Achologist?
content:
So what kind of person is an Achologist expected to be? The Achology Code of Ethics names 22 character traits as the essential personal and moral qualities of an Achologist. They rest on a smaller set of moral foundations, which are honesty, integrity, kindness, fairness, respect, responsibility and empathy, with trust treated as the basis of every professional relationship.

The 22 traits in full

  • Alertness, Attentiveness, Availability, Cautiousness.
  • Compassion, Cooperation, Courage, Diligence.
  • Discipline, Empathy, Enthusiasm, Flexibility.
  • Generosity, Honesty, Humility, Initiative.
  • Integrity, Orderliness, Patience, Positivity.
  • Resilience, Wisdom.

How the list is meant to be used

These are an aspirational inventory rather than a test. They are qualities to grow toward and to examine honestly in yourself, and nobody is expected to hold all 22 in equal measure. Read as a checklist they would only produce discouragement, which is the opposite of what they exist for.

The useful way to read them is one at a time. Availability, for instance, is a real question for anyone helping others while holding down a job, and Cautiousness is a genuine tension for a practitioner who wants to be useful quickly.

How these differ from the nine virtues

The traits overlap with the nine virtues of the Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC), and the two are easy to confuse, but they are separate instruments doing separate jobs.

The nine virtues are trained and tracked: each has its own live session, and holding eight of the ten current is a condition of progressing. These 22 traits are not tracked at all. They are held up as a description of the person the framework hopes you are becoming, and examined privately rather than assessed.

Why character is named at all

Most professional training describes only what a practitioner can do. Achology also describes who they are, because in helping work the two cannot be separated: a skilled practitioner who is careless with confidences, or impatient with people who are slow to change, does harm that technique cannot offset.

That reasoning is set out in full in why Achology emphasises character development. Alongside these traits sit the commitments every practising Achologist makes to clients, and the added standards that apply while you are still training. Between them they describe the practitioner the whole pathway is trying to produce.

title: What are the five principles of Achology's community?
content:
So what are the five principles you agree to as a member of Achology? Respect and Inclusivity, Active Engagement, Integrity and Professionalism, Ethical Conduct, and Shared Responsibility. They come from the Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC) and set the behavioural benchmark for how members treat one another and the space they share.

What each one means

  • Respect and Inclusivity: diversity enriches the community, every perspective is valued, and respect is treated as the basis of growth.
  • Active Engagement: learning is a shared effort, so members take part, listen with intention, ask thoughtful questions and give constructive feedback.
  • Integrity and Professionalism: trust is built through consistent honesty, accountability and professionalism, including upholding confidentiality.
  • Ethical Conduct: members respect others' rights, follow applicable laws, and contribute in ways aligned with the community's standards.
  • Shared Responsibility: the community is a collective effort, so issues are addressed collaboratively rather than left to sour.

What they look like on an ordinary day

These stop being abstractions the moment you are inside the community. Active Engagement is the member who reads a coaching post properly and gives a considered reply rather than a one-line reaction. Shared Responsibility is a group addressing a difficult thread openly and kindly instead of letting it fester. Integrity is somebody holding a confidence they were trusted with, months after the conversation.

None of that is dramatic. The principles describe the ordinary conduct that keeps a large learning community worth being part of, and the peer-learning culture is what they produce when they hold.

Why a learning community needs them stated

Because of what members are asked to do here. People practise coaching on each other, bring real difficulties to live sessions in front of a group, and receive honest feedback on work they are not yet good at.

None of that is possible without a floor under it. A member will not put a genuine problem into a room that might mock it, and will not take feedback from people who have not shown good faith. The five principles are the conditions the practice depends on, which is why they are written down rather than assumed, and why moderation exists to hold them.

They also govern disagreement rather than preventing it: how Achology approaches open disagreement covers that, and what to do if a discussion feels unsafe covers the case where the floor gives way.

How they sit alongside everything else

The five principles are part of the CCaC and work with the nine virtues it trains: the virtues describe the character to develop, the principles describe how to conduct yourself with others while you develop it.

They are the community-facing expression of the ten value commitments and the nine value-based principles, and they are distinct from the Community Code of Conduct, which is the platform's rulebook rather than a development framework.

title: Why does Achology's character code draw from Aristotle?
content:
So why does a modern psychology academy build its character code on Aristotle? Because that tradition treats character as something you develop rather than something you are simply born with or without. For a learning community whose whole premise is that people are capable of growth, a framework built on deliberate practice is the natural fit, and it is what the Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC) rests on.

What virtue ethics actually says

If the phrase is new to you, the idea behind it is plainer than it sounds. Most ethical systems ask what the rules are and whether you followed them. Virtue ethics asks a different question: what kind of person are you becoming.

Its answer is that good character is grown, through practice and honest effort, the same way any skill is. You are not born courageous or patient. You become so by acting that way, repeatedly, until it holds when it is inconvenient.

The idea of the middle point

Aristotle's particular contribution is that a virtue is not the opposite of a vice but the balanced point between two of them, one of excess and one of deficiency. Courage sits between recklessness and cowardice; generosity between wastefulness and meanness.

That structure is what makes the nine virtues usable in a session. Asked whether you are courageous, most people have no honest answer available. Asked which way you tend to lean, toward acting too fast or not acting at all, most people know immediately, and can say so in front of others without either boasting or confessing.

Why a rules-based code would not have worked

This is the part that explains the choice rather than merely describing it. Achology already has a rules-based instrument: the Code of Ethics governs professional conduct, and rules are exactly right for that job.

What rules cannot do is prepare somebody for the situations a helping practitioner actually meets, which are rarely covered by a clause. A rule tells you not to breach confidentiality. It does not tell you what to do when a client's difficulty exceeds your competence and they are asking you not to send them elsewhere. What settles that is the character of the person in the chair.

How it runs in practice

Each of the nine virtues is worked through in its own live session, with reflection questions rather than instruction, in the company of other members doing the same. Holding eight of the ten sessions current is what keeps your status green.

The recurring requirement is the philosophy applied to the timetable. If character is built by practice over time, a code you read once could never deliver it, which is why the CCaC repeats and why it is one of three separate codes rather than a section inside the ethics one.

title: What do the green and red CCaC statuses indicate?
content:
So what does it mean when your status shows green or red? They are the two states of your Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC) compliance. Green means at least 8 of your 10 CCaC sessions are current within a rolling 12-month period. Red means fewer than 8 are, and while you are red your progression on the pathway is paused until you restore it.

How you move between the two

Compliance is measured across a rolling twelve months rather than a fixed year, so sessions drop out of the window as time passes. Attend nothing for long enough and your count falls below eight on its own, without any decision having been made.

Coming back is the same mechanism in reverse. Attend enough sessions to bring the current count to eight or more and the status returns to green. There is no penalty period and no reapplication.

What red actually stops, and what it does not

Red pauses progression. It does not remove anything you have already earned, and it does not affect your access to courses, events or the community. Every credit and every level already verified stays exactly where it is.

What it means in practice is that further progress waits. Green status is a condition of advancing at every level from Achologist Adept upward, sitting alongside annual Code of Ethics training as the two ongoing compliance requirements.

Why the status exists at all

A status that can lapse is doing something a one-off certificate cannot. The CCaC treats character as built by examining yourself honestly, in good company, over time, so a member who worked through all ten virtue sessions three years ago and has not returned since is not in the same position as one who is still doing that work.

The colour is simply the visible form of that distinction. It keeps the character strand of the pathway a live commitment rather than something completed once and filed, which is the same reasoning behind the ethics training repeating annually and behind Master Achologist status having to be renewed each year.

Keeping it green without thinking about it

The sessions run regularly through the year and are one of the many kinds of live event open every week to every member of Achology. Members who attend as a matter of routine rather than tracking a count rarely see red at all, and choosing the right event for your level helps if you are deciding where to spend your time.

title: How many CCaC sessions do I need to complete, and how often?
content:
So how many character sessions do you need to complete, and how often? There are ten Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC) sessions in total: an introduction, plus one for each of the nine virtues. All ten are completed before you progress from Achologist to Achologist Adept. After that you keep 8 of the 10 current within any rolling 12-month period.

What one of these sessions is

A CCaC session is not a lecture on being good. Each virtue is worked through with a set of reflection questions, so the session is really an honest examination of where you actually sit on that virtue, in the company of other members doing the same. Courage, for instance, is treated as the point between recklessness and cowardice, and the session asks which way you tend to lean.

The sessions run regularly through the year, and they are one of the many kinds of live event that are open every week to every member of Achology, alongside the training and coaching formats that the live events article sets out in full.

What "keeping them current" means

The 8-of-10 requirement is ongoing rather than a hurdle you clear once. Because compliance is measured across a rolling twelve months, sessions gradually drop out of the window as time passes, so staying compliant takes steady engagement rather than a single burst of attendance. Leaving too long a gap is where members find themselves falling short without having decided to.

Holding 8 of 10 current is what keeps your status at green. Falling below eight turns it red, which pauses progression until it is restored, though nothing already earned is lost.

Why character is trained at all

This is the part that explains the rest. Most professional training develops only what you can do. The CCaC exists because Achology also attends to who you are becoming while you learn, on the plain view that a capable practitioner with poor character helps nobody.

That is also why it repeats rather than completing. Character, in this account, is not knowledge you acquire once. It is built by examining yourself honestly, over time, with people who will be straight with you, which is exactly what a rolling requirement protects and a one-off course could not.

Where it sits alongside everything else

The CCaC is the character strand of the pathway. Its counterpart is the professional strand, kept current through annual Code of Ethics training, and the two together are the ongoing compliance requirements at every level from Achologist Adept upward.

It is also one of three separate codes, which are easy to confuse: the Code of Ethics governs professional practice, the CCaC develops character, and the Community Code of Conduct governs behaviour on the community platform.

title: How do the Code of Ethics, CCaC, and Community Code of Conduct differ?
content:
So which code is which, and when does each one apply to you? Achology has three, and they are easy to confuse. The Code of Ethics governs professional practice, the Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC) develops character, and the Community Code of Conduct sets the rules for behaviour on the community platform.

What each one is

  • The Code of Ethics, formally the Ethical Framework for Practitioners of Applied Psychology, sets the standards of professional conduct expected of every practising Achologist. Annual training in it is a continuing professional development (CPD) requirement from Achologist Adept onward.
  • The CCaC is the character-development code: nine virtues trained through ten live sessions, forming the character strand of the pathway.
  • The Community Code of Conduct is the rulebook for the Circle community platform, governing how members behave in that shared space.

One situation, three codes

It helps to see them at work on a single moment. Imagine you are coaching another member in a live session and something sensitive comes up.

The Code of Ethics governs how you handle it professionally: confidentiality, your competence, the client's interests. The CCaC is the character behind that handling, the honesty and humility you bring to the room, which no rule can supply. The Community Code of Conduct covers how you conduct yourself in the group afterwards, in the shared space where other members can see you.

Why three rather than one

Because they answer three different questions, and a single document would answer all of them badly.

Rules work for professional obligations, where the standard has to be the same for everybody and enforceable. They do not work for character, which cannot be complied with, only developed, which is why the CCaC is a training programme with a status that can lapse rather than a document you agree to. And neither of those governs ordinary conduct in a busy online space, which needs plain house rules and moderation to hold them.

A simple way to hold the difference

The Code of Ethics is about how you practise with clients. The CCaC is about who you are becoming. The Community Code of Conduct is about how you treat other members day to day.

Two of the three, the Code of Ethics and the CCaC, are trained and tracked on the pathway and together form the two ongoing compliance requirements from Achologist Adept upward. The third simply governs conduct in the community space. Their practical expressions are the five commitments to clients and the five community principles.

title: What are Achology's 9 Code of Character and Conduct virtues?
content:
So what are the nine virtues you work through? The nine virtues of the Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC) are Courage, Temperance, Justice, Wisdom, Magnificence, Magnanimity, Friendliness, Truthfulness and Wittiness. Each has its own live session, and together with an introductory session they make up the ten CCaC sessions on the continuing professional development (CPD) pathway.

The nine, and the extremes each one sits between

The virtues come from Aristotle's virtue ethics, where a virtue is not the opposite of a vice but the balanced middle point between two of them, one of excess and one of deficiency. Read that way the list stops being abstract:

  • Courage sits between recklessness and cowardice.
  • Temperance sits between indulgence and joylessness.
  • Magnificence and Magnanimity sit between extravagance and meanness, in what you give and in how you carry yourself.
  • Friendliness sits between flattery and coldness.
  • Truthfulness sits between boastfulness and false modesty.
  • Wittiness sits between clowning and humourlessness.

Justice and Wisdom are treated differently in that tradition, as the qualities that govern the rest rather than as points on a spectrum of their own, which is why they are not described here as a middle between two extremes.

What actually happens in a virtue session

A session is not a lecture on being good. Each virtue is worked through with a set of reflection questions, so the ninety minutes is really an honest examination of where you sit on that virtue's spectrum, in the company of other members doing the same thing.

The middle-point idea is what makes that examination possible. Asked whether you are courageous, most people have no useful answer. Asked which way you tend to lean, toward acting too fast or not acting at all, most people know immediately.

Why character is trained rather than assumed

The virtues are treated as qualities developed through practice, not traits you either have or lack. That is the whole reason they are taught in recurring live sessions rather than written into a document members are asked to agree to.

It is also why the requirement never completes. Holding 8 of the 10 sessions current is what keeps your status green, and green is a condition of progressing from Achologist Adept upward.

Where this sits in the wider framework

The CCaC is the character strand of the pathway, running alongside the professional strand kept current through annual Code of Ethics training. It is one of three separate codes, and distinct again from the 22 character traits, which are aspired to rather than tracked.

title: What is the Achology Code of Character and Conduct (CCaC)?
content:
So what is the Code of Character and Conduct, and why does a psychology academy have one? The Code of Character and Conduct, or CCaC, is Achology's character-development code.
