title: Is there homework or assessment in Achology courses?
content:
So is there homework, and will you be assessed? Not in the traditional sense. Achology courses use reflective exercises, practice activities and self-assessment prompts rather than graded homework, and nothing is submitted for marking. Certificates of completion are issued for finished courses, and the emphasis throughout is on practical integration rather than academic testing.

What the exercises actually look like

Most courses include guided reflection: identify three situations where you responded defensively and what triggered it; describe a relationship pattern that repeats and the part you play in maintaining it; practise a communication technique in five real conversations and note what happened.

These exist to move the learning into your own life. They serve you rather than a grader, which is also why nobody checks whether you did them, and why the written materials are the half of a course most often skipped and most worth doing.

Why nothing is graded

Because a grade would measure the wrong thing and quietly change what you do.

An assignment written to be marked is written for the marker. It gets tidied, and the parts where you actually struggled get left out, which are precisely the parts the exercise was for. An honest answer to "describe a pattern you maintain" is not something anybody performs well for a score.

It also follows from how Achology treats learners. The teaching assumes capable adults who are here because they want the thing itself, and personal responsibility for your own learning is the stated expectation rather than a slogan.

Where you are actually assessed

There is assessment here, and it is nowhere near the coursework. It happens in the live practice.

When you coach another member while a group observes, or take a coaching role in a live session, you receive structured feedback from senior members, and every claim you make is independently verified before it counts. That is a far harder test than an essay, and it is what separates completing a course from being competent.

So the honest summary is that the courses are not assessed and the practitioner is. The two certificates record exactly that difference.

title: Do I need prior qualifications to study at Achology?
content:
So do you need qualifications to study here? No. There are no academic prerequisites, no psychology credentials required and no entrance requirements. The curriculum is designed for reflective, self-directed adults aged 18 and over, whatever their formal education. The only ordering requirements anywhere in the catalogue are two advanced practitioner courses that build on their own foundation courses.

What matters instead of credentials

  • Reflectiveness: the willingness to examine your own thinking, behaviour and assumptions honestly rather than defensively.
  • Maturity: the capacity to engage with challenging ideas, tolerate discomfort, and take responsibility for how you apply what you learn.
  • Consistency: applied psychology is practice, and practice rewards showing up.

None of those correlates neatly with degrees, which is exactly why degrees are not required. Who Achology is designed for describes the same character at more length.

Why it works this way

Achology's position is that psychological education should not be gatekept by academic institutions. Understanding human behaviour, developing self-knowledge and learning to help others are capacities adults can build directly, and how the subject came to be gatekept sets out the argument in full.

The Trust Statement describes the learner the environment assumes: an autonomous adult ready to be challenged. That is a real expectation rather than flattery, and why nobody holds your hand through it explains what follows from it.

What no entry requirement does not mean

It does not mean the standard is low, and it is worth separating the two, because they are routinely confused in this industry.

The gate is at the entrance in most education. Here it sits at the other end: progression past the first level requires demonstrated practice, independently verified, which no amount of prior study shortens. Anyone may begin. Nobody is waved through.

What your certificate is, regardless of your background

Educational recognition within Achology's framework. Not a statutory qualification, and nothing about your prior education changes what it is, in either direction. What a certificate proves is the honest account.

If you are entirely new to psychology, start with whether this suits a complete beginner.

title: Do I need to complete courses in a specific order?
content:
So do the courses have to be done in a particular order? No, for almost all of the curriculum. The courses are built for self-directed learning, so you take them in whatever order matches your needs. There are two exceptions, both advanced practitioner courses that assume their own foundation course came first.

The two that do have an order

  • The Neuro-Linguistic Programming Master Practitioner Course assumes you have completed Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP) Practitioner Training.
  • The Skilled Helper Practitioner Course (Advanced to Expert) assumes The Skilled Helper Training Course (with Prof. Gerard Egan) came first.

Each extends skills its foundation builds. Starting either without the earlier course means meeting material that assumes understanding you have not built yet, and the "Advanced to Expert" in the second one's own name says as much.

Everywhere else, you choose

Some natural progressions exist. The Diploma Course in Modern Applied Psychology (DiMAP) gives a broad foundation that makes later courses easier to absorb, which is why it appears in all seven schools, and the beginner course in each school opens its tradition before the practitioner courses deepen it.

These are recommendations rather than rules. Nothing stops you starting where your interest is strongest, and interest sustains study far better than sequence does.

Why so little is sequenced

Because the curriculum is organised by subject rather than by level, and because the teaching assumes capable adults who can judge their own readiness and adjust.

If a course turns out to assume ground you have not covered, the foundational course is there and your access to both lasts as long as you want it. Nothing is wasted by starting in what turns out to be the wrong place, which is exactly why an enforced sequence would cost more than it saved.

The one place order genuinely matters is not in the courses at all. The certification pathway is strictly cumulative, because it tracks demonstrated practice rather than study, and practice cannot be taken out of order.

Choosing your own path

If you are picking a first course, the strongest entry points are compared separately, and the three learning paths group the catalogue by goal rather than subject. The full list is on the courses page.

title: I'm overwhelmed by the options. How do I choose?
content:
So how do you choose when the options feel overwhelming? Answer one question rather than reading the catalogue: what specific challenge or goal matters most to you right now? Choose the single course that addresses that one thing, start it, and ignore everything else until it is finished. Clarity about what you need next comes from doing, not from planning the whole path in advance.

The one question, made concrete

Stop reading the full list and answer this instead: what problem am I actually trying to solve, or what skill am I trying to build, today?

Useful answers are specific. "I struggle in difficult conversations." "I keep repeating the same pattern and cannot see why." "I want to coach people properly rather than just listen well."

A specific answer points at one course. A vague one, "something interesting", points at all of them, which is the overwhelm talking rather than a decision waiting to be made.

Why the feeling is not a sign you are missing something

Twenty eight courses across seven schools is a lot to face at once, and the instinct is to map the whole thing before committing to any of it.

That instinct works for a syllabus and fails here, because the pathway is not sequential. Almost nothing has to be done in a particular order, and nothing requires prior qualifications. There is no wrong first step to avoid, which means the planning that feels responsible is mostly delay.

If no single answer surfaces

Then do not buy a course yet.

Membership at its introductory first-month rate lets you join the community, attend live events, and let a genuine interest surface from experience rather than from a list. The free tier costs nothing at all and gives the same first taste.

That is often the better route anyway: it is easier to know what you want to learn after watching people practise it.

Your first choice is not permanent

Nothing about a first course locks your path, access lasts as long as you want it, and you can change direction whenever you like. Where to start compares the routes, matched to different situations.

title: Which course should I take first as a complete beginner?
content:
So which course should you take first? One built as an entry point, and all of them assume zero prior psychology knowledge. For the broadest foundation, the Diploma Course in Modern Applied Psychology (DiMAP) introduces applied psychology across several traditions, Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) among them. For a focused start, the single-tradition courses open one field properly. For the smallest step, the Masterclasses tackle one topic each.

Match the entry point to what you want

The broad foundation. DiMAP is designed as a first major course: it builds the framework that makes every later course easier to absorb, appears in all seven schools, and is required by Senior Achologist I if you are heading toward accreditation. It suits somebody who wants the whole territory mapped before specialising.

A focused introduction. A Beginner's Guide to Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP), The CBT Toolkit: Core Principles and Real-World Applications, and Mindset Mastery each open one tradition. Choose whichever already interests you: interest carries beginners further than strategy does.

A short, single-topic start. The Masterclasses tackle one practical challenge each, from communication to self-discipline, and are the lowest-commitment way to test how Achology teaches before a larger course. How they differ from practitioner courses is worth two minutes.

The mistake worth avoiding

Choosing by which course sounds most impressive rather than by what you actually want to be able to do.

A beginner who picks the largest course because it seems most serious, with no particular question driving it, usually stalls in the third module. Somebody who picks a smaller course because it answers something they are genuinely stuck on tends to finish it and buy another. Choosing when the options feel overwhelming works that through.

Whichever you choose

Every purchase includes three months of membership, so your first course brings the community, live events and peer practice with it. Use them: they are half of what you paid for.

There is no required order after your first course either, and the full catalogue is at Achology courses.

title: Should I get membership first or buy a course first?
content:
So should you join first, or buy a course first? If you have a learning goal in mind, buy the course. Every course purchase includes three months of complimentary membership, so you get the structured content and the community together. Join first only if you want to explore the community before committing to a subject.

What a course purchase includes

The content itself, meaning video lessons, downloadable written resources and exercises, plus three months of membership: the community platform, live events, and the discussion spaces where other people are studying the same material.

After the three months, membership continues at the standard rate unless you cancel. It is a separate subscription from the course, so cancelling it never touches your course access, which lasts as long as you want it.

When membership first makes sense

If you genuinely do not know what you want to study yet, the introductory first month is the cheapest honest look inside: attend live events, watch how the community actually works, and choose a course from experience rather than from a sales page.

The free tier is cheaper still and gives real access, so there is a version of this that costs nothing at all.

One thing membership does not do is unlock courses. Those are purchased separately whichever order you choose.

Why the bundling exists at all

It is worth knowing that the three months is not a promotional sweetener, because that changes how you use them.

Achology's position is that watching a course does not make you competent, and that practice with other people is the half that does. Selling the course without the community would be selling the half that does not work on its own, which is why the two come together.

So the three months are not a trial to evaluate. They are the window in which the course you just bought is meant to be practised, and members who spend them only watching have used half of what they paid for.

Either order works

A course leads with structure and brings the community with it. Membership leads with the community and lets the course choice follow. If you are stuck because the catalogue feels like too much, start there instead.

title: Is Achology suitable for beginners with no background in psychology?
content:
So can you start here knowing nothing about psychology? Yes. Complete beginners can start anywhere in the curriculum: no prerequisites, no entrance exams, no requirement to prove existing knowledge. What success depends on is not prior study but the qualities that make learning possible, and those are not distributed by education.

No prior knowledge required

Whether you have never read a psychology book or hold an advanced degree, you enter on equal footing. The curriculum is built for self-directed adults and the beginner courses assume nothing.

That is deliberate rather than permissive. Achology's position is that understanding human behaviour and developing self-knowledge should not be reserved for people with formal academic training, which is the same argument behind requiring no qualifications and behind how the pricing works.

What actually decides whether you thrive

The students who struggle usually do not lack knowledge. They resist being challenged.

Applied psychology asks you to look at your own patterns, question assumptions you have held for years, and sit with ideas that may not flatter you. Beginners who arrive wanting new perspectives do well. People seeking confirmation of what they already believe find the material harder, and a degree does not help with that at all.

So the more useful question than "do I know enough" is "am I ready to be uncomfortable for a while". Who Achology is designed for describes that character, and who it is not for is the more honest read if you are unsure.

The advantage beginners actually have

Worth saying, because it is rarely believed by the person it applies to.

Somebody arriving without prior training has nothing to defend. They are not protecting a model they were taught, or a professional identity built on one school being right. In a curriculum that deliberately teaches several traditions without ranking them, that openness is worth more than a head start.

Where beginners usually begin

Several courses are built as entry points and assume zero prior knowledge, compared in which course to take first. If you would rather feel your way in before choosing, where to start compares the routes, and the free tier costs nothing.

title: Does Achology invite guest speakers?
content:
So does Achology bring in outside speakers to teach? No. There are no guest sessions, guest workshops or drop-in modules inside the member space. It is a standing governance decision rather than an oversight, made to keep the quality, consistency and accountability of the teaching environment in Achology's own hands, and it sits with the Trust Statement and the Terms and Conditions.

The reasoning

Achology holds explicit standards for how psychology is presented, discussed and applied. External teaching introduces variables that are difficult to verify or govern at scale:

  • How influence is used in a room, and what is modelled by the person using it.
  • How confidently ideas are asserted, and with what caveats.
  • The risk of commercial self-promotion, even where it is unintended.
  • The safety of reflective spaces in which members are often candid.

None of that is a judgement on any outside practitioner's quality. It is a practical decision about what Achology can responsibly validate and remain accountable for.

Why the last point carries the most weight

Because of what actually happens in these rooms. A member in a HOT Seat brings a real difficulty and is coached on it in front of the group. A character session asks people to examine honestly where they fall short.

Those things only work when everyone present is inside the same standards and answerable to them. A visiting speaker, however good, is a person the community has no way to hold to the Code of Ethics afterwards, and the members who would carry the cost of that are the ones who spoke most honestly.

Who does teach, then

Instruction comes from Achology's own instructors and curriculum, and the learning runs through the community's structured formats: live training, peer practice and mentorship, led within its own standards.

Members learn a great deal from each other, which is a different thing from external teaching and is the point of the peer-learning model. Where the boundary sits on peer guidance is covered in who is responsible for advice from other members, and members who want to teach grow into it from inside.

title: Can I share or redistribute Achology course content?
content:
So can you pass course material on to somebody else? No, not the materials themselves. Under the Terms and Conditions, course materials may not be copied, recorded, reproduced, distributed, shared, sold, sublicensed, or rebroadcast, in whole or in part, in any format, whether for commercial or non-commercial purposes, without Achology's prior written permission. What you are warmly encouraged to share is what you learn: the ideas, frameworks, and skills are yours to use and pass on in your conversations, your practice, and your work.

What you can do with course content

You can study the materials as often as you like through your account, download the written resources (PDFs, worksheets, templates) for your own reference, and keep them permanently. You can take notes, build summaries, reference the frameworks in discussions and practice sessions, and apply everything you learn in your professional practice. That application is the entire point of the training.

What you cannot do

You cannot pass the materials themselves to others: no forwarding PDFs, uploading content to other platforms, reselling, lending, or reproducing any of it without written permission. Video lessons stream on the platform and are not downloadable at all. The prohibition covers non-commercial sharing as well as commercial: giving a worksheet away breaches the Terms just as selling it would.

The distinction that matters

Achology's teaching exists to be used. Teach what you have learned, coach with it, explain a framework to a colleague, and credit where it came from. The line sits between the knowledge, which is yours once you have learned it, and the copyrighted materials that carry it, which remain Achology's. If you have a genuine case for using materials beyond personal use, ask first at support@achology.com; written permission is the lawful route the Terms provide.

title: I found Achology content on a torrent site. Is it legitimate?
content:
So you have found Achology content on a torrent site: is it real? It is real content, and it is pirated. All Achology material is copyrighted, and anything on torrent sites, file-sharing platforms or unauthorised third-party websites is neither authorised nor supported. Under the Terms and Conditions, course materials may not be copied, distributed or rebroadcast in any format without written permission.

What the copyright covers

Everything Achology produces: course videos, written materials, handbooks and frameworks. Video lessons stream on the platform and are deliberately not downloadable; written resources are provided for enrolled students' own use. Distributing any of it, commercially or not, needs written permission, which a torrent upload plainly does not have.

Why a pirated copy misses most of what it looks like

This is the part worth understanding before deciding it is a bargain, because even a complete set of the video files captures a fraction of what a purchase is.

It cannot include the community where the skills are actually practised: the live sessions, the peer coaching, the mentorship groups. It cannot include the certification pathway, because progression there is independently verified rather than self-declared. It does not receive course updates, so it decays from the day it was uploaded.

And it misses the point of the teaching itself. Achology's whole position is that watching the material is not the thing that makes you competent. Practising it with real people who tell you honestly how it went is. A downloaded copy is precisely the half that does not work on its own.

The legitimate route

Every course is available individually, in school bundles, or through the Access All Areas Pass on the courses page, and each purchase includes three months of membership. If cost is the barrier, the free tier gives genuine access to events, the coaching board and the forum without payment, and the Knowledge Hub is free to read.

If you have seen content being distributed without permission, it can be reported to support@achology.com.

Related questions

  • Can I share or redistribute Achology course content?
  • Can I share my Achology account or login with someone else?

title: Can I share my Achology account or login with someone else?
content:
So can you let somebody else use your login? No. Each purchase grants access for one individual only. The Terms and Conditions require you to keep your account details confidential and not to share, transfer or allow access by any other person. Breaching that is grounds for Achology to end the contract, and no refund applies where access ends for that reason.

What the rule covers

One purchase, one person, one set of credentials. No sharing a login with a partner, lending an account to a friend, letting a colleague log in to watch a module, or running a shared household account.

If somebody else wants to learn, they need their own account and purchase. Every course page carries its own checkout, and the free tier costs nothing if the obstacle is money.

Why the rule exists, and it is not only revenue

There is a commercial reason and a more important one.

The commercial reason is that single-user access is what keeps the courses viable at their price. Shared accounts erode the model that keeps the education affordable and open to anybody.

The more important reason is what an account is here. It is not a key to a video library. It is the record of one person's practice: sessions attended, coaching delivered, claims independently verified. Two people behind one login make that record a fiction, and the fiction would sit underneath a certificate somebody later shows a client.

What happens if it is breached

Under the Terms, Achology may end the contract where the content and account rule is materially breached. Access can be withdrawn and money already paid is not refunded in that situation, which the suspension article sets out in full.

Keeping your credentials to yourself also protects you, since you are responsible for activity on your account. That matters more than it sounds in a community where members arrange one-to-one coaching sessions with each other.

title: Is Achology responsible for advice I get from other members?
content:
So who is responsible if another member gives you bad advice? You are, for what you choose to act on. Achology does not assess, supervise, endorse or guarantee the quality or outcomes of coaching, feedback or guidance you receive from other participants. Peer practice sessions are learning activities rather than professional services, and responsibility for what you accept from them stays with you.

What the policies say

The Terms and Conditions state that practice events involve members meeting to rehearse coaching or helping skills, and that these are practice-only learning activities.

The Disclaimers add that Achology does not supervise peer interactions, does not verify members' competence, and does not endorse advice shared between them. The Trust Statement carries the reasoning: members learn with and from one another, and collaboration does not remove personal accountability.

Why this is not Achology stepping back

It reads like a disclaimer and is closer to a description of what peer practice is.

The member coaching you is learning, by design. The pathway requires it: nobody reaches a verified level without practising on other members, and everybody practising was once being practised on. A session where the coach is still developing is not a lapse in the system, it is the system, and pretending otherwise would misrepresent it to both people in the room.

What is supervised is the environment rather than the content: the spaces are moderated for respect and integrity, and trainees are required to say they are training.

What this means in practice

Treat what you hear in peer sessions as practice material from a fellow learner rather than professional advice. Take what is useful, leave what is not, and keep your own judgement in the room.

If you need medical, psychological or mental health support, the Disclaimers direct you to qualified professionals, and in the UK to NHS 111 or Samaritans. Achology does not provide crisis support, which is stated plainly rather than buried.

One further boundary

If you exchange contact details or collect personal information from other members during events, you do that independently and are responsible for your own compliance with data protection law. Achology does not control that processing.

title: How do Achology's trust and legal policies work together?
content:
So how do all these policy documents fit together? Achology publishes seven policy documents designed to be read as a single framework, with the Community Code of Conduct alongside them: each covers one dimension of the relationship between Achology and its learners, and each cross-references the others. The Disclaimers carry a map of how they fit together, and no document is meant to be read in isolation.

What each document covers

  • Terms and Conditions: the contractual mechanics, your order, access rules, cancellation rights, and liability.
  • Refunds Policy: the financial boundaries, including the 14-day money-back guarantee and its scope.
  • Privacy Notice: what personal data is collected, why, and your rights over it.
  • Cookie Policy: cookies and tracking on the website.
  • Trust Statement: the working philosophy on responsibility, boundaries, and who the environment is for.
  • Disclaimers: the scope limits, what Achology does not provide, and reliance boundaries.
  • Accessibility Statement: the access commitment.
  • Community Code of Conduct: the conduct standard for the learning community, named in the Terms as part of the entire agreement.

How they connect

The Terms are the contractual spine: their entire-agreement clause names the Trust Statement, Disclaimers, and Community Code of Conduct as part of the agreement, and the Refunds Policy forms part of the Terms directly. Where the Terms and the Refunds Policy are ever inconsistent, the Terms state that they prevail, except where consumer law requires otherwise. Your statutory rights sit above all of them, covered in What are my legal rights as an Achology customer?

Where to start reading

Start with the document that owns your question: money in the Refunds Policy, data in the Privacy Notice, conduct in the Community Code of Conduct, boundaries in the Disclaimers and Trust Statement. Each will point you to the others where they overlap.

  • What law governs Achology's terms and conditions?

title: What happens if Achology updates a course I've bought?
content:
So what happens to a course you own when it gets updated? The updated content appears automatically in your account at no extra cost, replacing the previous version. You never repurchase a course to receive its improved form. Minor changes happen without notice; where a significant change materially affects something you bought, the Terms and Conditions require reasonable notice and an explanation of your options.

Minor changes

Compliance with changes in law or regulation, and technical adjustments to functionality, reliability, performance and security.

These do not materially affect your access or the nature of the service, so no advance notice is required. Fixing a broken link or improving video quality sits here.

Significant changes

Updating, revising or replacing course content. Changing the availability, structure or delivery of courses. Changing, replacing or discontinuing certification programmes.

Where such a change materially affects your access to something you have already purchased, reasonable notice is given and your options explained, which may include ending the contract.

Why updating is normal here rather than exceptional

Because the curriculum is maintained as a living body of teaching rather than published once and archived.

That follows from how the subject is treated: a course that never changed would be a course nobody was still teaching. In practice it means what you bought tends to be worth more in three years than on the day you bought it, which is unusual for a one-off purchase.

Why streaming means you always see the current version

Video lessons stream on the platform, so every student watches a lesson as it stands now. Written resources you have already downloaded remain yours, which is worth knowing in both directions: your saved worksheets do not change under you, and your saved worksheets also do not update.

If a change ever leaves you unhappy with a purchase, your statutory rights and the Refunds Policy both apply, and what happens if the platform itself changes is answered separately.

title: What law governs Achology's terms and conditions?
content:
So whose law applies if something goes wrong? Scots law governs Achology's Terms and Conditions. If you live in the United Kingdom, any dispute arising from your contract goes to the courts of the part of the UK where you live. If you live outside the UK, disputes fall under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Scottish courts.

Why Scots law

Because Achology is a Scottish business. It operates through two Scottish-registered companies, Achology Transactions Ltd (SC697126) and The Academy of Modern Applied Psychology Ltd (SC612822), both registered at Clyde Offices, 2nd Floor, 48 West George Street, Glasgow, as set out in the registered company details.

Choosing the law of the home jurisdiction is ordinary commercial practice rather than a position being taken. For most learners the practical difference is small, because the core consumer protections come from UK-wide legislation such as the Consumer Rights Act 2015, which applies whichever legal system governs the contract.

Where a dispute would go

If you live in England, Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland, you bring a dispute before the courts of your own part of the UK. If you live outside the UK, the Scottish courts have exclusive jurisdiction.

In practice almost nothing reaches a court. Contact support@achology.com first, and the routes for ending a contract or asking for money back are already published: the refund policy, the 14-day guarantee and cancelling at any time exist so that most disagreements have an answer before they become disputes.

Your statutory rights are not affected

This is the part worth being clear about, because a governing-law clause looks like it might take something away and does not.

It decides which legal system interprets the contract. It does not remove your consumer protections, and nothing in Achology's own policies reduces them either. Your rights as a customer apply on their own terms regardless of what any policy says.

That is also why the answer is published at all. A company that intended to lean on the fine print would have little reason to explain where the fine print stops, and how the policies fit together is written on the same principle.

title: What are my legal rights as an Achology customer?
content:
So what are you legally entitled to as a customer? UK consumer law protects you when you buy from Achology, on top of Achology's own policies. Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, all Achology products count as digital content, which must be as described, fit for purpose, and of satisfactory quality. If content falls short, you may be entitled to a repair or replacement, and where a fault cannot be fixed, a full or partial refund. The Terms and Conditions state directly that nothing in them removes your statutory rights.

The three standards digital content must meet

As described. The content must match what the order page says it contains; those details form part of your agreement with Achology.

Fit for purpose. The content must do what digital content of its type is reasonably expected to do: courses deliver structured learning material, videos play, downloads open.

Of satisfactory quality. The content must meet the standard a reasonable person would expect of it.

The remedies if something is faulty

If digital content is faulty, you are entitled to a repair or replacement first. If the fault cannot be fixed, or is not fixed within a reasonable time and without significant inconvenience, you may be entitled to a full or partial refund. If you can demonstrate that faulty digital content damaged your device and Achology did not exercise reasonable care and skill, you may be entitled to a repair or compensation. These rights are subject to conditions and exceptions set out in law.

How this sits alongside Achology's own policies

Achology's Refunds Policy, including the 14-day money-back guarantee, is a commercial promise that operates alongside your statutory rights, never instead of them. Where the two differ, the law wins. For independent guidance on your statutory rights, contact Citizens Advice.

title: Does Achology use automated decision-making or profiling?
content:
So does anything here make automated decisions about you? No. Achology does not use personal data for automated decision-making or profiling that produces legal effects, or similarly significant effects, on individuals, as those terms are defined under UK GDPR. Decisions about access, participation and services are made with human involvement. The Privacy Notice states this directly.

What the two terms actually mean

They sound interchangeable and are not.

Automated decision-making is a decision made about you entirely by a system, with nobody reviewing it and nobody able to override it. Automated credit scoring and algorithmic job-application screening are the familiar examples.

Profiling is the automated analysis of personal data to evaluate or predict something about you, such as your behaviour, interests or likely choices.

UK GDPR gives people specific protections wherever either one produces legal or similarly significant consequences, which is the threshold this answer turns on.

What Achology's position covers

No algorithm alone decides whether you can enrol, progress or reach any content, and no system scores or categorises you in a way that carries legal or similarly significant consequences.

Standard website analytics and cookies operate for performance and security, described in the Cookie Policy, and are a separate matter from making decisions about individuals.

The one place a judgement is genuinely made about you is the verification of professional development claims, and that is deliberately the opposite of automated: every claim is reviewed by committee members who are experienced practitioners, which is exactly why the record means anything to somebody outside Achology.

Why this is worth stating at all

Because in online education a great deal now is automated: what gets recommended to you, what a platform predicts you will buy, and in some cases who is quietly filtered out. Saying plainly that none of that happens here is only useful if it is checkable, which is why it sits in the published Privacy Notice rather than in marketing copy.

It also fits the wider position: personal data is not sold, and it is shared only with the parties needed to run the service.

Your rights if this ever changed

If processing of this kind were ever introduced, the UK GDPR protections would apply, including the right to obtain human intervention, to express your point of view and to contest a decision. Questions about your own data can go to support@achology.com at any time, and you can request deletion of your account and data.

  • Who does Achology share my personal data with?

title: Can I request the deletion of my Achology account and data?
content:
So can you have your account and data deleted? Yes. Email support@achology.com and ask for your personal data to be erased. The right exists under UK GDPR and the Privacy Notice confirms it. Achology responds within one calendar month, and some records may lawfully be kept where tax, legal or regulatory obligations require it.

How to request deletion

Email support@achology.com stating that you want your personal data erased, and include your name, the email address on your account, and enough detail for your records to be found accurately.

No legal wording is needed. "Please delete my Achology account and all personal data you hold about me" is enough. The contact form works equally well.

Cancelling is not deleting

This is the part most people get caught by, so it is worth stating plainly. Cancelling your membership stops future payments. It does not erase your data, and it is not treated as a deletion request.

If you want both, ask for both, separately. They are handled by different processes for a good reason: a member who cancels and returns eighteen months later usually wants the progress record they built to still be there, and deleting it by default would destroy exactly that.

What happens next

Achology responds within one calendar month. If the request is complex the period can be extended by up to two further months, and you must be told of the extension and the reason within the first month. If any part is refused, Achology must explain which lawful exemption applies.

What may be kept

Most personal data falls in scope for deletion. What may lawfully remain is data covered by statutory retention rules, such as tax and financial records, and data reasonably needed to establish or defend legal claims. Those are the same grounds described in how long data is kept.

If you are not satisfied

Raise it with Achology first at support@achology.com. If it stays unresolved you have the right to complain to the UK's supervisory authority, the Information Commissioner's Office.

  • What personal data does Achology collect about me?
  • Can I cancel my Achology membership anytime?

title: How long does Achology keep my personal data?
content:
So how long does Achology hold on to your data? Only for as long as it is needed for the purpose it was collected. As a general framework, data is kept for the length of your relationship with Achology and, in most cases, for up to five years afterwards, then securely deleted or anonymised unless a legal obligation requires longer. The framework is set out in the Privacy Notice.

The general framework

Where data is needed to provide services, it stays for the duration of the relationship. The five-year window afterwards allows Achology to keep proper business records, maintain security, meet legal and regulatory obligations, and defend legal claims if a dispute arises.

Once that window closes and no other criterion applies, the data is securely deleted or anonymised. Nothing is kept indefinitely, which is the part worth taking from this answer.

What decides the period for a given piece of data

Retention varies by category. The Privacy Notice names six factors:

  • Contractual requirements: data needed to run your account and provide what you hold.
  • Legal and regulatory obligations: tax, accounting and audit rules that set statutory periods.
  • Legitimate business needs: record-keeping, security and service improvement.
  • The nature and sensitivity of the data: riskier data is not held longer than necessary.
  • Your relationship and activity: whether you remain an active member or customer.
  • Disputes and legal claims: data that may be needed to establish or defend a claim.

Why a five-year figure rather than a vague assurance

Because a stated period is checkable and a reassurance is not. It sits with the other things about Achology that can be verified without anyone's cooperation: the registered company numbers, the learning provider registration, and the published policies themselves.

It also follows from the position elsewhere: data is not sold, it is shared only with the parties needed to run the service, and nothing here makes automated decisions about you.

If you want your data removed sooner

You can ask at any time rather than waiting for a period to expire. How that works, and what may lawfully be kept, is in requesting deletion of your account and data.

  • Can I request the deletion of my Achology account and data?

title: Who does Achology share my personal data with?
content:
So who else gets to see your data? Only the parties needed to run the services: payment and financial providers, cloud and technology providers, service contractors, professional advisers, fraud prevention services, group companies, and public authorities where the law requires it. Every recipient processes data under Achology's instructions for defined purposes, and none receives it for their own marketing. The categories are published in the Privacy Notice.

The recipients, category by category

  • Group and joint controllers, including Kain Ramsay Limited, where relevant to providing courses, events or related services.
  • Payment and financial providers: processors and accountants handling transactions, billing and tax compliance.
  • Service providers and contractors: IT, marketing support, administration and technical support, working under instruction.
  • Technology and cloud providers: the hosting and software that run and secure the platforms.
  • Professional advisers: lawyers, accountants and auditors, for legal or regulatory purposes only.
  • Fraud prevention and security services, where needed to prevent misuse or unauthorised access.
  • Public authorities and regulators: HMRC, law enforcement and courts, only where disclosure is required or reasonably necessary by law.
  • Business transfers: selected parties in any future sale, merger or restructuring, with safeguards in place.

Why the list is this long, and why that is reassuring

A short list would be the suspicious one. Running an online academy means a payment processor, a hosting provider and an accountant at minimum, and any organisation claiming to share data with nobody is either not operating or not telling you everything.

What matters is the shape of the list rather than its length. Every category above is operational, legal or regulatory. None of it is commercial: no data brokers, no advertising networks, no partners receiving members in exchange for services.

The safeguards behind the sharing

Third parties processing data on Achology's behalf do so only under its instructions, bound by confidentiality and data protection obligations.

Where a provider sits outside the UK, transfers happen only with appropriate safeguards under UK GDPR, such as adequacy recognition or approved contractual protections. That matters here because the membership is worldwide while the companies are Scottish.

What is never shared

Data is not sold, and not shared with any third party for that party's marketing. Nothing here profiles you or makes automated decisions about you either, and how long anything is kept is published alongside.

title: Does Achology sell my personal data to third parties?
content:
So does Achology sell your data? No. Achology does not sell personal data, and it does not share personal data with third parties for their own marketing purposes. The Privacy Notice states both commitments directly. Data goes to specific service providers only where that is necessary to run the platform and deliver what you bought.

Why it takes two commitments rather than one

Because a bare promise not to sell your data is a weaker sentence than it sounds.

Some platforms use a narrow reading of selling that leaves room to hand data to advertising networks or partner companies in exchange for services rather than cash. Stating both positions, no selling and no sharing for third-party marketing, closes that gap. Your data does not reach external marketing operations whether or not money changes hands.

What sharing does happen

Running an online education platform involves service providers: payment processing, cloud hosting, IT support. Each handles data only under Achology's instructions, for defined operational purposes, under confidentiality and data protection obligations.

The full picture is in who Achology shares data with, and how long anything is kept is published alongside it.

Marketing from Achology itself

Achology may send information about courses or events similar to what you have bought or asked about, and newsletters where you subscribed. You can opt out at any time from the unsubscribe link in any email, or by contacting support@achology.com. Opting out does not affect access to anything you have purchased.

Why this position and not another

Because of what members bring here. People discuss real difficulties in mentorship groups, bring genuine problems to live coaching sessions, and practise on each other.

A community that asks for that kind of honesty cannot also be quietly monetising who its members are. It is the same reasoning behind nothing here profiling you or making automated decisions about you: the conditions have to be trustworthy before the practice can be real.

title: What personal data does Achology collect about me?
content:
So what does Achology actually know about you? Achology collects the personal data needed to run your account, deliver your courses, process payments, and operate its learning community: contact details, account and registration information, transaction records, communications, technical usage data, and marketing preferences. It does not intentionally collect special category data such as health information, ethnicity, religious beliefs, or political opinions. The full list is set out in the Privacy Notice, and what Achology actually holds about you depends on how you use the platform.

The categories, in plain terms

The Privacy Notice lists the categories of personal data Achology may collect. Not every category applies to every person.

  • Contact information: your name, postal address, email address, and telephone number.
  • Account and registration details: login credentials, profile information, and account activity.
  • Transaction and service information: courses purchased, events attended, certifications awarded, and credits earned.
  • Communications: emails, support enquiries, and other correspondence with Achology.
  • Images and recordings: photographs, video, or audio from events where recording takes place and participants have been informed.
  • Technical and usage data: device and browser information collected through cookies, explained in the Cookie Policy.
  • Marketing preferences: your choices about receiving communications.
  • Financial information: payment details, handled securely and in most cases processed by third-party payment providers rather than stored by Achology.

Two further categories apply only in specific situations: recruitment information if you apply for a role, and business or professional information where it is relevant to the services provided.

Special category data is not collected

Achology does not intentionally collect what UK data protection law calls special categories of personal data: health information, racial or ethnic origin, religious or philosophical beliefs, political opinions, trade union membership, genetic or biometric data, or sexual orientation. If you volunteer something of that kind yourself, for example in a community discussion, it is not used for any specific purpose and is handled under the Privacy Notice.

Where this is set out

The Privacy Notice is the full statement of what is collected, why, and on what lawful basis. If you have a question about your own data, contact support@achology.com or use the contact form.

title: Where can I find the resources for my course?
content:
So where are the resources that came with your course? Inside the course itself. Log into your Achology account, open the course, and its content is organised by module and lesson: the video teaching, and alongside it the written resources, PDFs, worksheets and exercises, each attached to the lesson it belongs to. Work through in order or jump to the section you need.

What downloads and what streams

The written resources download freely, so save the worksheets and reference materials as you go. Video lessons stream inside the platform and cannot be downloaded, which is also what guarantees you are watching the current version whenever a course is updated. The downloads article has the full picture.

One habit worth forming

Download a lesson's written materials while you are studying that lesson, not later.

Materials gathered as you go arrive already organised by the learning they belong to, and you will remember what each one was for. Materials gathered in a batch at the end are a folder of files nobody opens again. Over a practitioner course that difference is the whole value of the written half of the course.

Why the worksheets matter more than they look

This is worth saying plainly, because the videos feel like the course and the worksheets feel like the extras. It is closer to the other way round.

Achology teaches that completion and competence are different things, and the exercises are where the second one starts. Watching a lesson tells you what a technique is. Working the sheet is the first time you apply it to a real situation, which is the step the live practice then builds on. Members who skip the written work tend to be the ones who finish a course and wonder why nothing changed.

If a course you bought is not showing

Check that you are logged in with the same email address you purchased with. A mismatch between the purchase address and the login address is the commonest cause by a wide margin.

If the addresses match and the course is still missing, the missing course article covers the remaining checks and what to send support.

title: Can I direct message other Achology members?
content:
So can you message another member privately? Yes. Open any member's profile by clicking their name, then use the message icon to start a private conversation. Direct messages work on desktop and in the community app, and they are how members arrange peer practice, follow up after live events, and build one-to-one connections around what they are learning.

What direct messages are actually for

Some of the most useful learning here happens one to one: arranging a coaching practice session from The Coaching Board, debriefing after a live event that went sideways, or continuing a thread with the one member it really concerned.

Reaching out is normal and welcomed. A message that says why you are writing lands well: naming the course you are both working through, or the session you were both in, gives the other person something to reply to. A bare hello usually does not.

Why this matters more here than on most platforms

Because the pathway itself runs on one-to-one work. Peer coaching sessions have to be arranged between two members before they can happen, and nobody progresses far without asking somebody they have never spoken to for an hour of their time.

So the first message you send to a stranger here is not an imposition. It is the ordinary mechanism of the place working, and the member receiving it is usually looking for the same thing.

The standards travel with the message

Private does not mean unaccountable. The conduct expectations that govern the public spaces, set out in the Community Code of Conduct, apply in direct messages too, and the moderation standards cover both.

Some members switch messaging availability off in their settings. That is a privacy choice to respect rather than a fault to work around, and it is worth reading as a boundary rather than a rebuff. Connect through their posts or at an event instead.

If messaging is not working

If you cannot send or receive at all, the cause is almost always an availability setting rather than a technical fault, and the messaging troubleshooting article walks through the checks. If a conversation has become uncomfortable, what to do when something feels unsafe is the route.

title: How do I create posts in the Achology community?
content:
So how do you post something in the community? Open the discussion space your post belongs in, select New Post, write it and publish. The editor supports formatted text, images, video embeds and tagging other members, and you can edit a post after publishing from its own menu, so nothing you share is set in stone.

Writing the post

Choose the space first, because that is what decides who sees it. The editor works like any modern rich-text editor, and typing a forward slash in the body brings up the formatting options. When you finish, publish immediately or save a draft to come back to.

If you tag a member they are notified, so tag the people your post genuinely concerns rather than tagging for attention.

What to post, and what makes a post work

Insights from your course study, honest questions, reflections on practice, and replies to other members all count, and the replies are worth as much as the posts.

The quality of what comes back tracks the specificity of what you put in. "Can anyone help with confidence?" sits unanswered because nobody knows what help you need. The same question with the situation in it, what you tried and where it went wrong, gets answers from people who have been there. How to ask a question and get useful answers covers that properly.

A good first post is simply what you are studying and what you are working toward. The replies usually make the second one easy.

Why posting is part of the learning rather than beside it

This is the part worth understanding before you decide you are too new to contribute. Achology teaches that competence is built by practising in company and receiving honest feedback, which is why the teaching is built around peer learning.

Writing out what you are working on, and having somebody question it, is the cheapest version of that available. Members who only read tend to finish courses; members who post tend to change how they practise. Nobody is expected to sound expert, and the culture is built for people mid-way through learning something.

After publishing

You can edit or delete your own post at any time from its menu. The moderation standards apply to every space, and how disagreement is handled here is worth knowing before your first contested thread.

  • Can I direct message other Achology members?

title: How do I manage my Achology community notifications?
content:
So how do you get the notifications under control? Open your profile menu in the community and select Notifications. From there you control which activity triggers an alert, how each is delivered, in-app, email or push, and, most usefully, you can set preferences per space, so the groups that matter speak up and the rest stay quiet.

The per-space control is the one that matters

Global settings are blunt: all or nothing. Per-space settings are how members make the community liveable.

The pattern that works is opting fully into the few spaces central to your development, typically your mentorship group and the events space, and muting the spaces you only browse. Ten minutes of per-space choices removes most of the noise permanently, and it is the single adjustment that stops people drifting away from the community without ever deciding to.

Matching delivery to importance

A useful default:

  • Push, through the phone app, only for what should genuinely interrupt you: event start times and direct messages.
  • Email for what you want a record of, such as replies to your own posts.
  • In-app for everything else, waiting for you next time you visit.

What is actually at stake

This looks like housekeeping and is not. Too many alerts and you start ignoring all of them, including the one reminder that mattered. Too few and you find out about a session after it ran.

Either way the thing you lose is the same: attendance at the live events, which is the only part of membership that cannot be caught up on later and the part your progression actually depends on. A member who misses events is not behind on reading, they are not progressing.

Revisit as your use changes

What suits a new member browsing widely rarely suits an active member practising in two groups. Revisit the settings whenever your pattern shifts.

If something specific misbehaves, such as email notifications that are switched on but never arrive, the notification problems article covers the fixes.

title: How do I set up my Achology community profile?
content:
So how do you set up your profile? Click your profile picture in the community, choose Edit profile, and work through the fields: a clear headshot, a headline saying who you are and what you are working on, your timezone, a short bio, and any links you want to share. Five minutes here pays back for as long as you are a member.

The fields worth doing properly

  • The photo makes you recognisable across discussions and live events. A clear, friendly headshot is enough.
  • The headline sits beside your name everywhere, so make it say something real. "Counselling student building a coaching practice" beats "Member".
  • Your timezone makes event times display correctly, which matters because the events run on UK time.
  • The bio is where a practice partner decides whether to approach you. Say what you are studying, what you are working toward, and what kind of connection you would welcome.

Why this matters more here than on most platforms

Because of how the pathway works. Progression depends on peer coaching sessions that have to be arranged between two members, and on practice that other people agree to take part in.

Nobody progresses far without a stranger deciding to spend an hour with them. Your profile is what that decision is made on. An empty one does not make you invisible so much as unreadable, and members quietly skip past it when they are looking for somebody to practise with.

This is the same reason a specific question gets better answers than a vague one. In a community built on peer practice, being legible to other members is not vanity, it is the mechanism.

Your privacy choices

The profile settings also hold your privacy preferences: whether your email is visible, whether members can send you direct messages, and whether you appear in the member directory.

Set these deliberately rather than leaving the defaults. They decide how findable and contactable you are, and you can change any of them at any time.

title: How do I download the Achology community app?
content:
So how do you get the community onto your phone? Download Circle's free app from the App Store on iPhone and iPad, or Google Play on Android, then log in with the same email address and password you use for your membership. That is the whole setup, and it takes about two minutes.

Step by step

  • Open the App Store or Google Play and search for "Circle - Community Platform". The app is free.
  • Install it, open it, and log in with your Achology membership email and password.
  • The community appears exactly as it does on the web, arranged for the smaller screen.

You get the whole thing: discussions, events, messaging, notifications and your profile. Circle is the platform the community runs on, which is why the app is not called Achology.

Why the app is worth having rather than optional

Because of the one thing you cannot catch up on later.

Most of the community waits for you. Discussions sit there, resources stay in your course, recordings appear where they exist. The live events do not. They run at a time, and the practice your progression actually depends on happens inside them.

The app is the reliable route for push notifications, so event reminders and direct messages reach you wherever you are, which the mobile browser does not handle well. It also makes joining a session on the move straightforward rather than a scramble.

Once installed, set which activity is allowed to interrupt you, because the useful setting is a narrow one: event start times and direct messages, and little else.

If login fails in the app

Use the exact email your membership is registered with. A different address is a separate account, and that is the commonest cause of everything looking empty.

If the password will not cooperate, reset it from the login screen and check spam for the reset email, which comes from Circle rather than from Achology. The reset article covers the rest.

title: What is Circle, and why does Achology use it?
content:
So what is Circle, and why is the community built on it? Circle is a community platform built for learning organisations, and it is what the Achology community runs on at community.achology.com. Discussions, live events, peer practice, direct messages and your member profile all live there, in one place, on the web and through free mobile apps.

Why a dedicated platform rather than a Facebook group

Plenty of online learning communities live in Facebook groups or Slack channels. Those tools are good at what they were built for, general social connection and workplace chat, but a learning community needs different things: scheduled live events, structured spaces, member profiles built around development, and conversation that stays findable a year later.

The difference shows up most in the events. Achology's 22 live event types have to be scheduled, joined, attended and then claimed for credit, and a chat tool has nowhere to put any of that.

What it means for you day to day

The practical difference is attention. Circle carries no advertising, no algorithmic feed and no sponsored content competing with the thing you came for, so what you see is the community's actual activity in the order it happened.

That is not a small point for a psychology academy. A community about attention and self-direction, hosted somewhere engineered to capture both, would be teaching one thing and demonstrating another.

One login covers everything, the mobile app brings it to your phone with push notifications, and your notification settings decide how much of it reaches you.

The one thing to know about it

Because the community sits on a separate platform from this website, signing in crosses two domains. That is invisible almost always, and occasionally it is the reason a login fails on a browser with strict cookie settings. The login article covers it, and which browsers work best covers avoiding it.

Getting oriented

If you are new, three things cover the start: installing the app, setting up your profile, and joining your first discussion or event. After that the community explains itself by use.

  • How do I set up my Achology community profile?

title: How do I join a live Achology community event?
content:
So how do you get into a live event when it starts? Log into the community at community.achology.com, in your browser or the app, open Upcoming Events, RSVP to the one you want, and at the scheduled time open its page and click join. Event times are listed in UK time, so convert to your own before planning around one.

Before the session

RSVP as soon as you decide, and add it to your own calendar with the time already converted.

The timezone conversion is the single commonest reason people miss sessions they meant to attend, and it catches experienced members as often as new ones because UK time shifts twice a year while their own may not. Setting your timezone on your profile makes the calendar display correctly and removes most of the arithmetic.

Read the description's theme paragraph too, so you know what this particular session covers and whether preparation is expected. For skill workshops that means studying the named lesson first.

Joining smoothly

Arrive a couple of minutes early and check your setup. When the browser or app asks for microphone and camera permission, grant it: a dismissed prompt is the commonest cause of turning up with no audio, and the audio and video checks cover the rest.

Early arrival matters more in the practice formats than it looks, because sessions such as coaching practice organise pairs and roles in the first minutes. Joining late is not just late for you.

If you cannot find the event

If the events space itself is missing rather than one session, the likely causes are that your membership access is not active or you are logged in with a different email address from the one on your purchase. The missing space article covers both before you assume the event has gone.

Sessions run daily across the community, so if one clashes with your day, another of the same type is rarely far away. What runs lists all 22 formats.

title: How do I contact Achology support?
content:
So how do you actually get hold of the support team? Three routes reach them. The fastest is the enquiries page, which sends your message to the right team. You can also phone +44 (0)1383 344 086 or email support@achology.com. Whichever you use, putting your account details in the first message is what gets most issues resolved in a single exchange rather than three.

Choosing the route

  • The enquiries page suits almost everything: account issues, membership, billing, access problems and general questions, as well as partnership and media enquiries.
  • Email suits anything where you want a written thread, and screenshots travel well with it.
  • The phone suits anything easier to explain out loud than to type. Achology is based in Scotland, so the line runs on UK hours.

What to have ready

Five things: the email address your account is registered with, your device and browser, the exact action you attempted, what happened instead, and a screenshot of any error. What to include in a support request explains why each one matters.

Never put your password or full card details in a message. Support does not need them and will never ask for them.

Try the article first, if there is one

Not to deflect you, but because it is usually faster. The commonest problems have their own answers and most are settled in under a minute: not being able to log in, a reset email that has not arrived, and a course that is not showing account for most of what reaches support, and all three have a common cause you can check yourself.

One route to skip

Posting an account problem in the community's discussion spaces reaches other members rather than the support team, and account issues usually involve details you should not post publicly. Go direct instead.

title: Which browsers and devices work best with the Achology community?
content:
So which browser or device should you be using? Any modern browser reaches the Achology community, which runs on Circle at community.achology.com. Chrome and Firefox give the most consistently reliable experience across every feature, including live events. On phones and tablets, the free community app is the better route than a mobile browser.

On a computer

Keep your browser current, whichever you use. An out-of-date browser sits behind a great many otherwise mysterious faults, and it is the first thing worth checking before assuming something is broken.

For live sessions, Chrome and Firefox handle the audio and video features most dependably. A stable connection matters more than the power of the machine, so a modest laptop on good broadband will serve you better than a fast one on a weak signal. Circle also offers a desktop app if you would rather work outside the browser.

The Safari and iPhone exception

Safari works for general browsing, but it has a known third-party cookie behaviour on iOS that can block logins, and it is worth knowing about in advance because it does not look like a cookie problem when it happens. It looks like the login screen simply returning you to itself.

The reason is structural rather than a fault: the community runs on a separate platform from the main site, so signing in involves a second domain, which is exactly what strict cookie settings are designed to interrupt. Using Chrome on the same device is the workaround, and the login troubleshooting article covers the rest.

On a phone or tablet

Install the community app rather than relying on the mobile browser. It is free, it handles push notifications properly, which the browser route does not, and it makes joining an event on the move straightforward.

That matters more here than on most platforms, because the thing you would miss is a live session. Achology's events run through the week and are the part of membership that has to be attended rather than caught up on. Installing the app takes a couple of minutes.

The short version

Chrome or Firefox on a computer, the community app on your phone, everything kept updated, and a stable connection for live events. If something still misbehaves, audio and camera problems have their own article.

title: What should I include in an Achology support request?
content:
So what should you put in a support request to get it sorted quickly? Five things: the email address you log in with, your device and browser, the exact action you attempted, what happened instead of what you expected, and a screenshot of any error. A request carrying all five usually gets resolved in one exchange rather than a back-and-forth of questions.

The five, and what each one does

  • Your login email identifies the account immediately, and is the single most useful line in the message.
  • Device and browser, such as "Windows laptop, Chrome" or "iPhone, community app", tells support which environment to reproduce.
  • The exact action, such as "tried to join the 7pm workshop from the event page", narrows where to look.
  • What actually happened: a blank screen, an access denied message, or nothing at all.
  • A screenshot of the error, which removes all ambiguity about what you are seeing.

Why the email address matters most

Because it is the cause of the problem far more often than it is merely the identifier.

Two addresses belonging to the same person are two separate accounts as far as access is concerned, and that single fact sits behind most of what reaches support: failed logins, courses that will not appear and reset emails that never arrive. Naming the address you are using, and the one on your receipt if they differ, often answers the question before support opens it.

One more helpful line, and one caution

If you have already tried a different browser or device, say so and what happened. It saves support suggesting the step you have done.

Never include your password, full card number or any other credential. Support does not need them and will never ask for them, which is worth knowing as a rule rather than a courtesy: any message that does ask is not from Achology.

Why this works

"It's not working" forces a first reply made entirely of questions, and that is one round trip lost before anything is looked at. Handing over the five items turns your first message into everything needed for a diagnosis. How to reach support gives the three routes.

title: Achology invite link not working?
content:
So your invite link is not working? The likely causes are an expired link, a link already used once, even partially, or a browser setting stopping the joining flow from completing. Invite links on Circle can be time-limited, single-use or revoked, so one that worked before may simply no longer be valid.

The checks, in order

  • Clear your browser's cookies and cache, then try the link in a fresh session.
  • On Safari and iOS, third-party cookie settings are a known cause of join failures. Trying Chrome on the same device is a quick test.
  • If you started the joining flow earlier and abandoned it partway, the link may already count itself as used, in which case retrying will never revive it.

The cookie point is structural rather than a bug: joining crosses from this site to the community platform, which is exactly the kind of thing strict cookie settings are built to interrupt. Which browsers work best covers avoiding it altogether.

Whatever you do, do not create a second account

This is the important part of the answer, and it is the reason this article exists rather than a one-line fix.

When a link will not work, the obvious move is to give up on it and sign up fresh with a different email address. That single decision creates the problem behind most missing courses and spaces: one account holding what you paid for, another that you can actually log into, and nothing visible in either.

Untangling two accounts afterwards takes considerably longer than waiting for a replacement invite. A broken link is an inconvenience of minutes. A duplicate account is an inconvenience of days.

Getting a fresh invite

Contact support, say the invite link is not working, and include the email address the invite was sent to and what happens when you click it. A replacement resolves nearly every remaining case.

How to reach support gives the routes, and what to include keeps it to one exchange.

title: Can't see your Achology course or community space?
content:
So you have paid but cannot see your course: what is going on? Almost always an email mismatch: you are logged into the community with a different address from the one you bought with. The second most common cause is access not yet applied to your account. Both are usually fixed within minutes.

Check the email match first

Find your purchase receipt and note the address on it, then check which address you are logged in with. If they differ, log out and back in with the purchase email.

Two addresses belonging to the same person are still two separate accounts as far as access is concerned. That single fact is behind the majority of what reaches support, including failed logins and reset emails that never arrive.

If the emails match

Some spaces are restricted and need access assigned to your account, and a brand new purchase can take a short time to provision. Give it a little time.

Note too that some spaces are deliberately invitation-only, so a space you cannot see is not always a space you are missing. Spaces, groups and events work differently, and groups in particular are joined rather than opened.

Whatever you do, do not sign up again

The instinct when something you paid for will not appear is to create a fresh account and start over. That converts a five minute fix into a genuine tangle: one account holds everything you bought, the other is the one you can log into, and untangling them takes far longer than a support message.

If it still is not there

Contact support with three things: your purchase receipt, the email you log in with, and the specific course or space you cannot see. That combination lets support find the mismatch immediately, usually in one exchange.

How to reach support gives the routes, and nothing you have bought is at risk in the meantime. Access is attached to your purchase, not to your session, and it lasts as long as you want it.

title: Can't send or receive direct messages in the Achology community?
content:
So you cannot send or receive a direct message? The cause is almost always a messaging availability setting, either yours or the other member's, rather than a technical fault. Circle, the community platform, gives every member control over whether they can be messaged directly, and those settings can block messaging in both directions without showing an obvious error.

Check your own setting first

Open your profile or account settings in the community and find your direct messaging availability. If it is switched off, nobody can message you, and in some configurations you cannot start conversations either. Switch it on and test with a member you know.

This is the fix in most cases, and it is easy to have switched off without remembering: the setting sits alongside the notification controls that most members adjust when they first join.

If your setting is on and it still fails

Then the other member has most likely disabled theirs, which is their privacy choice working exactly as intended rather than a fault to report. Arrange contact another way: reply to one of their posts, or speak to them at a live event.

Community-level settings can also restrict who may send direct messages. A restriction that applies to everyone is policy rather than a problem with your account.

Why members can switch messaging off at all

Because of what people bring here. Members practise coaching on each other, discuss real difficulties, and take part in live sessions where somebody brings a genuine problem. A community where anyone can be messaged privately, by anyone, at any time, is a community where some members would take part less honestly.

Giving each member that control is part of the same thinking as the community principles: the conditions have to be safe before the practice can be real. So a closed inbox is not a slight, and it is worth reading as a boundary rather than a rejection.

If nothing explains it

Contact support with your login email and the name of the member you tried to message. What to include in a support request covers the rest, and what to do if an interaction feels unsafe is the separate route if that is the real issue.
